timeline.title: Manasota people fish and hunt the bay
timeline.text: Archaeologists call the people who lived on the central Gulf coast of the Florida peninsula from about 500 BCE the Manasota culture; around 900 CE it developed into the Safety Harbor culture. Weedon Island Preserve says Manasota people hunted and fished the bay and left shell mounds along the coast, and it shows a 39.9-foot pine dugout canoe, about 1,100 years old, that was excavated from its shoreline in 2011.
timeline.notes: Year -500 = 'about 500 BCE' (Wikipedia, Manasota culture). Canoe facts (Manasota makers, 12.17 m / 39.9 ft pine dugout, excavated 2011, 1,100 years old, shown in the Welcome Center) from the Pinellas County preserve page; its radiocarbon line is garbled on the page ('AD 690 l 1010') so no radiocarbon date is given here.

timeline.title: Safety Harbor culture takes shape around the bay
timeline.text: From about 900 CE until after 1700, people on the central Gulf coast of Florida practiced what archaeologists call the Safety Harbor culture, named for the large platform mound at Safety Harbor. Their towns had temple mounds, plazas and shell middens; the Tocobaga who met the Spanish belonged to this culture.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'from about 900 CE until after 1700'. The NHL nomination calls Safety Harbor the type site of the Safety Harbor phase. Temple mound/plaza/midden description: Wikipedia History of Tampa ('These small coastal villages contained a temple mound, a central plaza, and one or more shell middens').

timeline.title: A Tocobaga village on Boca Ciega Bay
timeline.text: People of the Safety Harbor culture lived at the Jungle Prada Site on Boca Ciega Bay in today's west St. Petersburg for about 600 years, from about 1000 to 1600 CE. Most of the mounds that once lined the bay here were used as fill in the 20th century; a plaza mound and a long midden mound survive, partly in the city's Jungle Prada de Narvaez park.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia (citing Simpson 1998 and the 2002 NRHP registration form by Robert Austin): Tocobaga inhabited the site 'from 1000 to 1600 CE'; NRHP listed Feb 4, 2003 (ref 03000007). Coordinates: census match for 1700 Park St N (the park's address area), checked against the Photon match 'Jungle Prada' park (27.787904,-82.753495). No place record for the park exists in other slices yet.

timeline.title: Tocobaga's capital at Safety Harbor
timeline.text: The Safety Harbor Site in Philippe Park, a flat-topped shell mound about 20 feet high on Old Tampa Bay, was occupied from late prehistoric times into the early Spanish period (about 1500 to 1650). It is thought to be the capital of the Tocobaga, and it was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1964; Pinellas County says the temple mound is the largest remaining mound in the Tampa Bay region.
timeline.notes: NHL nomination (NPS, revised June 1981): 'late prehistoric site which was occupied into the early part of the Spanish period (ca. 1500-1650 A.D.)'; mound 'about 150 feet in diameter and about 20 feet in height'; 'generally thought that the Safety Harbor Site may be the Tocobago capitol'. NHL year 1964 from Wikipedia Safety Harbor site. Pinellas County page: 'largest remaining mound in the Tampa Bay region'.

timeline.title: Narváez expedition lands on Boca Ciega Bay
timeline.text: In April 1528 Pánfilo de Narváez landed with 300 men in Boca Ciega Bay, about 15 miles north of the entrance to Tampa Bay, at what is known as the Jungle Prada Site in today's St. Petersburg. On May 1 he split the expedition, sending about 300 men north overland while the ships sailed up the coast; the fleet searched for the land party for nearly a year and never found it.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: spotted land April 12, 1528; 'Narváez landed with 300 men in Boca Ciega Bay at what is known as the Jungle Prada Site'; split into land and sea contingents May 1, 1528. Pinellas County facts page: the area 'was discovered by Panfilo de Narvaez in 1528'. The exact landing place is traditional, hence 'traditionally'. History of Tampa (Wikipedia): 'they abandoned their camp after only a week... A dozen years later, a surviving member of the expedition named Juan Ortiz was rescued by Hernando de Soto's expedition.' | Verifier 2026-09-27: removed 'after about a week' (the article gives April 12 sighting and the May 1 split) and 'a dozen years later de Soto rescued a survivor, Juan Ortiz' (Ortiz was from the naval force, not a survivor of the land party; he has his own record).

timeline.title: De Soto's men find Juan Ortiz
timeline.text: Juan Ortiz came to Tampa Bay in 1528 on a ship searching for the missing Narváez expedition and was captured by the people of Uzita, a Safety Harbor culture chiefdom on the bay's south shore near the mouth of the Little Manatee River. After escaping to the neighboring chiefdom of Mocoso he lived there until the de Soto expedition found him in 1539; he then served the Spanish as an interpreter.
timeline.notes: Juan Ortiz (captive): 'In 1528 Juan Ortiz was on a ship searching Tampa Bay for any sign of the Narváez expedition'; 'found by the de Soto Expedition when they landed in Tampa Bay in 1539'; 'Ortiz could speak the languages of both Uzita and Mocoso'. Uzita (Florida): chief town near the mouth of the Little Manatee River, in the Ruskin area; part of the Safety Harbor culture. No coordinates: the town site is not fixed by the sources.

timeline.title: Hernando de Soto's army lands in Tampa Bay
timeline.text: In May 1539 Hernando de Soto's army of soldiers, hired mercenaries, craftsmen and clergy made landfall in Tampa Bay and met fierce resistance from the people defending their homelands. The expedition went on for four years and about 4,000 miles across the Southeast; De Soto National Memorial in Bradenton, created in 1948, commemorates it.
timeline.notes: NPS home page: 'In May 1539, Conquistador Hernando de Soto's army of soldiers, hired mercenaries, craftsmen, and clergy made landfall in Tampa Bay... a four year, four thousand mile odyssey'. basicinfo: 'Created in 1948, the park's mission is to commemorate the 1539 expedition'. The exact landing site is not stated by NPS; the point is the memorial.

timeline.title: Menéndez visits Tocobaga and leaves a garrison
timeline.text: In 1567 Pedro Menéndez de Avilés visited the Tocobaga town that was almost certainly the Safety Harbor Site and left about 30 soldiers there. When Spanish boats brought supplies in January 1568 they found the town deserted and the soldiers dead.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia Tocobaga: 'The name Tocobaga first appears in Spanish documents in 1567, when Pedro Menéndez de Avilés visited what was almost certainly the Safety Harbor site'; 'Leaving a garrison of 30 men at Tocobaga'; 'In January 1568... found the town deserted, and all the Spanish soldiers dead.' NHL nomination: 'visited in 1567 by Pedro Menendez who left a small detail of soldiers there for several months.'

timeline.title: Florida becomes British, and the bay is renamed Hillsborough
timeline.text: Great Britain acquired Florida in 1763 at the end of the Seven Years' War, and under British rule the bay was renamed Hillsborough Bay for Lord Hillsborough, secretary of state for the colonies; the name survives in the Hillsborough River and County. Native people and Cuban fishermen kept a seasonal camp at the mouth of Spanish Town Creek in today's Hyde Park, smoking mullet to sell in Cuba. Spain regained Florida in 1783.
timeline.notes: All from Wikipedia History of Tampa, section 'English rule'. No coordinates: the Spanish Town Creek mouth is not geocodable reliably. | Verifier 2026-09-27: the article says 'Indians and Cuban fishermen' lived in the seasonal encampment; wording adjusted.

timeline.title: Cuban fishing ranchos work the 'Coast of Tampa'
timeline.text: By the mid-1700s fishermen from Havana sailed each fall and winter to Florida's Gulf coast, whose main fishing ground was the 'Coast of Tampa', including Tampa Bay and Charlotte Harbor; they salted mullet, drum and other fish and hired Native people as guides and crews. A British review of the fishing in 1767-1768 found it no threat, and by the late 1700s year-round camps called ranchos stood between Tampa Bay and Estero Bay, until the U.S. Army removed their residents during the Second Seminole War.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. Fishing ranchos article: 'By the 1740s, Cuban fishermen were employing guides...'; 'The primary fishing area was the "Coast of Tampa", including the "Port of Tampa" (Tampa Bay) and the "Port of Sanibel" (Charlotte Harbor)'; 'A review of the fishing operations in 1767-1768 concluded that these operations were not a threat to the British'; 'By late in the 18th century, year-round fishing stations, known as ranchos, were established along the Florida coast between Tampa Bay and Estero Bay'; Second Seminole War removal. Year 1767 is the first dated event in the account. No coordinates: the ranchos lined a long coast.

timeline.title: Spain hands Florida to the United States
timeline.text: The United States acquired Florida from Spain in 1821 for $5 million; Hillsborough County says the area had been under the rule of Spain, France, Great Britain and the United States between 1559 and 1819. One of the first U.S. actions in the new territory was the raid that destroyed Angola, the Maroon settlement on the Manatee River.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27 (scope item '1821 cession'). HCFL: 'Between 1559 and 1819, the area now called Florida was under the rule of four nations: Spain, France, Great Britain and the United States. The United States purchased Florida from Spain in 1821 for $5 million.' History of Tampa: 'In 1821, the United States purchased Florida from Spain... One of the first U.S. actions in its new territory was to launch a raid which destroyed Angola'. No coordinates (statewide).

timeline.title: Angola, a maroon community on the Manatee River, is burned
timeline.text: Angola was a Maroon community of 600 to 750 people who had escaped slavery, on the Manatee River and Sarasota Bay. In 1821, as the United States took over Florida, Andrew Jackson sent Creek allies to raid it and the settlement was burned; survivors fled, some as far as Andros Island in the Bahamas. Artifacts from the Angola era have been found at Manatee Mineral Springs Park in Bradenton, which the National Park Service added to its Network to Freedom in 2019.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia Angola, Florida: 600-750 residents, maroons and Black Seminoles; Jackson as territorial governor in 1821 ordered Creek allies to raid; 'burned to the ground'; survivors to Cape Florida and the Bahamas (Red Bays, Andros); Manatee Mineral Springs Park excavations since the early 2000s; NPS Network to Freedom 2019. Hillsborough County: 'The United States purchased Florida from Spain in 1821 for $5 million.' Coordinates: Photon match for Manatee Mineral Springs Park, Bradenton. | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'farming community of several hundred' replaced by the article's figure (historian Canter Brown Jr.: 600 to 750 people).

timeline.title: Fort Brooke is founded at the mouth of the Hillsborough River
timeline.text: Col. George Mercer Brooke arrived at Tampa Bay with James Gadsden and four companies of infantry on Jan. 18, 1824, and the post, first called the camp on the Hillsborough River, was established on Jan. 22. The Tampa Bay History Center calls Fort Brooke the genesis of modern Tampa; the fort stood about where the Tampa Convention Center is today.
timeline.notes: TBHC: 'Established on January 22, 1824', 'first known simply as the camp on the Hillsborough River', 'arguably the genesis of modern-day Tampa'. City Clerk: 'January 18, 1824 - Col. Brooke, along with James Gadsden and four companies of infantry, arrived in Tampa Bay.' Wikipedia History of Tampa: the fort was 'just about where today's Tampa Convention Center sits downtown'. Coordinates: Cotanchobee Fort Brooke Park (Photon), the commemorative park beside the Convention Center; history-of-tampa places the fort itself beneath the Convention Center block.

timeline.title: Hillsborough County is organized
timeline.text: On Jan. 25, 1834, the Legislative Council of the Territory of Florida organized Hillsborough as Florida's 19th county, named for Wills Hill, Lord Hillsborough. At statehood in 1845 it still covered what are now Pinellas, Polk, Manatee, Sarasota and several other counties, with only 836 residents counted, not including soldiers or Native Americans.
timeline.notes: County history page: 'takes its name from Wills Hill, British Secretary of State to the Colonies from 1768-1772'; 'On Jan. 25, 1834, the U.S. Legislative Council for the Territory of Florida approved an act organizing Hillsborough as Florida's 19th county'; statehood 1845 extent; population 836. 'Lord Hillsborough' from Wikipedia History of Tampa.

timeline.title: Dade's command, marching from Fort Brooke, is destroyed
timeline.text: In December 1835 Maj. Francis Dade's column of 110 men left Fort Brooke on the military road to Fort King, near today's Ocala, and on Dec. 28 it was ambushed by Seminole warriors; 108 were killed. The battle started the Second Seminole War, which lasted until 1842, and Fort Brooke became a refuge, depot and staging area.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia Dade battle: date December 28, 1835; 'The battle sparked the Second Seminole War, which ended in 1842'; survivor Pvt. Sprague reached Fort Brooke on New Year's Day 1836. History of Tampa: ambush 'while they were on their way from Fort Brooke to Fort King (near present-day Ocala)'; Fort Brooke 'first served as a refuge for settlers, then as a vital military depot and staging area.' Infobox: strength 110, casualties '108 killed, 1 wounded'; 'companies of 110 men... departed from Fort Brooke... heading up the Fort King military road'. Pinned at Fort Brooke (where the march began); the battlefield is in Sumter County outside the guide's areas.

timeline.title: Fort Foster guards the Hillsborough River crossing
timeline.text: Col. William S. Foster and 430 men built Fort Foster in 1836 to defend the bridge crossing on the Hillsborough River during the Second Seminole War; it was garrisoned on and off from December 1836 to April 1838. A reproduction stands on the original ground across U.S. 301 from Hillsborough River State Park.
timeline.notes: Hillsborough River State Park Preservation Society: 'reproduction of a fort originally built on the same grounds in 1836 by Col. William S. Foster and his 430 men'; 'utilized during the Second Seminole War to defend the bridge crossing at the Hillsborough River'; 'garrisoned on and off from December 1836 through April 1838'; 'across from the park' on U.S. 301. Coordinates: Photon historic=archaeological_site 'Fort Foster'. | Verifier 2026-09-27: coordinates moved 2.7 km from an OpenStreetMap archaeological-site node on Lostine Road to the NRHP/Wikipedia point (28 8 57 N, 82 13 11 W), which the around-daytrips slice also uses; the preservation society places the fort on U.S. 301 across from the park.

timeline.title: The war ends and settlers take up Pinellas land
timeline.text: The Second Seminole War ended in 1842, and the federal Armed Occupation Act of that year offered 160 acres to settlers who would bear arms and farm the land. That year Odet Philippe acquired 160 acres at today's Safety Harbor; he is described as the first permanent non-Native settler of the Pinellas peninsula, and his plantation is now Philippe Park, the oldest park in Pinellas County.
timeline.notes: Odet Philippe (Wikipedia): 'first permanent, non-native settler on the Pinellas peninsula... acquiring 160 acre of land in what is today Safety Harbor in 1842'; buried in Philippe Park, his former plantation, 1869. Clearwater (Wikipedia): 'Federal Armed Occupation Act of 1842 offered 160 acre to anyone who would bear arms and cultivate the land'. Pinellas County: 'the oldest park in Pinellas County'. Wikipedia Safety Harbor gives a conflicting 1823 date for Philippe; the 1842 date of the Philippe article is used.

timeline.title: Robert Gamble starts a sugar plantation on the Manatee River
timeline.text: Maj. Robert Gamble took up 160 acres under the Armed Occupation Act and arrived on the Manatee River in 1844; his mansion, built about 1845-1850 with tabby walls two feet thick, anchored a sugar plantation that grew to 3,500 acres on which Gamble likely enslaved more than 200 people. Confederate cabinet member Judah P. Benjamin stayed there in May 1865 before fleeing Union forces and sailing to England; the house is now a state historic park in Ellenton.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. Wikipedia: 'received 160 acres for homesteading under the Armed Occupation Act, and arrived at the Manatee River site in 1844'; 'Built 1845-1850'; 'the forced-labor farm included 3,500 acres, and Gamble likely enslaved more than 200 people'; 'two-foot-thick walls are constructed of tabby'; Benjamin 'stayed at the plantation in May 1865, before fleeing from the Union forces and sailing to England'. floridastateparks.org returns 403 to WebFetch. Point from the around-daytrips/history-region place record.

timeline.title: The Great Gale of 1848 wrecks Fort Brooke and Egmont Key's new light
timeline.text: In late September 1848 the strongest hurricane known to have struck the Tampa Bay area made landfall near today's Clearwater. Only five houses were left standing in Tampa, all damaged, and most of Fort Brooke was destroyed; the surge covered Egmont Key with about six feet of water, damaging the lighthouse built there that year, and cut the inlet at John's Pass.
timeline.notes: 1848 Tampa Bay hurricane (Wikipedia): 'the strongest known hurricane to impact the Tampa Bay area'; landfall 'near modern-day Clearwater in Pinellas County on September 24' (the infobox runs Sept 23-28). History of Tampa: 'Every building in Tampa was either damaged or destroyed, including most of Fort Brooke.' Egmont Key Light: 'In September 1848 a hurricane covered the island with six feet of water and damaged the new lighthouse.' | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'every building in Tampa was damaged or destroyed' restated as the article's 'only five houses were left standing ... all damaged'; added the John's Pass inlet (same article, and the Madeira Beach article) and the johns-pass-village link.

timeline.title: Tampa incorporates as a village
timeline.text: On Jan. 18, 1849, fourteen men voted unanimously to establish the Village of Tampa with a trustee government, and a week later they elected five trustees. Citizens organized the Town of Tampa on Sept. 10, 1853.
timeline.notes: City Clerk: 'January 18, 1849 - 14 men vote unanimously to establish Tampa Village with a trustee form of government.' 'January 25, 1849 - Village of Tampa elects 5 trustees with M.G. Sikes elected president.' 'September 10, 1853 - Citizens vote to organize as the Town of Tampa'. Coordinates: the history-of-tampa point for the incorporation event (27.9475, -82.457), the original downtown.

timeline.title: Oaklawn, Tampa's first public burial ground, opens
timeline.text: Oaklawn Cemetery, Tampa's oldest cemetery and first public burial ground, dates from 1850. With the adjoining Catholic St. Louis Cemetery it covers about three acres downtown and holds Tampa's first mayor, Judge Joseph B. Lancaster, 12 other mayors, a Florida governor and two Florida Supreme Court justices, and it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2017.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. City page: 'As Tampa's oldest cemetery, originating in 1850...'; 'Tampa's first public burial ground'; 'approximately three acres'; 'Tampa's first Mayor, Judge Joseph B Lancaster, and 12 other City of Tampa mayors, one Florida governor, and two Florida Supreme Court justices'; 'In the same year [2017], Oaklawn Cemetery received a designation on the National Register'. Point from the history-tampa place record.

timeline.title: Tampa receives its first city charter
timeline.text: Citizens voted on Sept. 15, 1855 to replace the town government with a city charter, and on Dec. 15, 1855, Gov. Broome signed the act of the Florida Legislature chartering the City of Tampa. The city's modern charter dates from July 15, 1887, when it absorbed the Town of North Tampa.
timeline.notes: City Clerk: 'December 15, 1855 - Governor Broome signs Special Act of the Florida Legislature granting a charter for the City of Tampa.' 'July 15, 1887 - City of Tampa organizes under special act... abolishing the governments of the Town of Tampa and Town of North Tampa and establishing the charter for the City of Tampa.'

timeline.title: The present Egmont Key lighthouse is lit
timeline.text: After the 1848 hurricane damaged the first Egmont Key lighthouse, rebuilding began in 1857 and the present tower went into service in 1858 with a new Fresnel lens. In the 1850s the island was used to hold Seminole prisoners before they were shipped west to Indian Territory.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia Egmont Key Light: 'The current Egmont Key Light dates from 1858'; 'In 1857 work was begun rebuilding the tower. The reconstruction was completed in 1858, and the lighthouse was placed back in service with a new third order Fresnel lens'; 'In the 1850s Egmont Key was used as a temporary holding area for Seminoles before they were shipped to the Indian Territory.' Coordinates: Photon match 'Egmont Key Light' (man_made=lighthouse).

timeline.title: A Union gunboat shells Confederate Tampa
timeline.text: Florida seceded on Jan. 10, 1861, Confederate troops manned Fort Brooke, and the Union Navy blockaded the mouth of Tampa Bay, using Egmont Key as a base. On June 30 and July 1, 1862, the gunboat USS Sagamore demanded the fort's surrender and then shelled the fort and town in the Battle of Tampa; neither side suffered real damage or casualties. A marker in Oaklawn Cemetery shows where a shell fell.
timeline.notes: Battle of Tampa (Wikipedia): fought June 30-July 1, 1862; USS Sagamore steamed into Tampa Bay to demand the surrender of the Confederate garrison at Fort Brooke. History of Tampa: secession Jan 10, 1861; 'Fort Brooke was soon manned by Confederate troops'; blockade near the mouth of Tampa Bay; 'The Battle of Tampa on June 30-July 1, 1862 was inconclusive'; image caption 'Marker in Oaklawn Cemetery where a shell fell during the Battle of Tampa.' Egmont Key Light: 'Union forces captured the island in July 1861 and used it as a base'. Coordinates: Oaklawn Cemetery (Photon). | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'inconclusive' removed (Wikipedia's infobox says Confederate victory; its text says neither side inflicted real damage).

timeline.title: Union raiders burn blockade runners on the Hillsborough River
timeline.text: On Oct. 16, 1863, the Union gunboats Tahoma and Adela began shelling Fort Brooke as a diversion; on Oct. 18 about 100 Union troops landed at Ballast Point, marched 14 miles north and burned James McKay's blockade runners Scottish Chief and Kate Dale on the Hillsborough River near today's ZooTampa at Lowry Park. When Union forces landed again in May 1864, the fort was no longer garrisoned, and they occupied the town briefly.
timeline.notes: Battle of Fort Brooke (Wikipedia): 'fought October 16-18, 1863'; Tahoma and Adela 'began a slow bombardment of Fort Brooke'; 'When Union forces again landed in May 1864, Fort Brooke was no longer garrisoned and the town had been virtually abandoned.' History of Tampa: troops 'headed a few miles up the Hillsborough River until they found McKay's hidden blockade runners Scottish Chief and Kate Dale near present-day Lowry Park Zoo and burned them'; occupation of May 1864 left after three days. Coordinates: Lowry Park (Photon). | Verifier 2026-09-27: the troops landed at Ballast Point and marched north (not 'up the Hillsborough River'); text adjusted to the article.

timeline.title: St. Petersburg's first Black settlers make a homestead
timeline.text: John Donaldson and Anna Germain, the first Black settlers in what became St. Petersburg, arrived in 1868 and built a homestead at what is now 18th Avenue South and 31st Street South. The city says that for 20 years the Donaldsons were the only African American family in present-day St. Pete.
timeline.notes: City of St. Petersburg history page, verbatim facts. No coordinates (an intersection only).

timeline.title: John C. Williams buys the land that becomes St. Petersburg
timeline.text: In 1875 John Constantine Williams of Detroit bought 2,500 acres of waterfront land on the lower Pinellas peninsula. Thirteen years later he traded part of it to Peter Demens so that Demens's Orange Belt Railroad would reach his settlement.
timeline.notes: City of St. Petersburg: 'In 1875 John Constantine Williams of Detroit, Michigan moved to Tampa and bought 2,500 acres of warm waterfront land that would eventually become St. Petersburg. Thirteen years later, he transferred part of that land to Peter Demens... In exchange, Demens extended the Orange Belt Railroad to Williams's settlement.'

timeline.title: Settlers arrive at Spring Bayou, soon named Tarpon Springs
timeline.text: A. W. Ormond and his daughter Mary, the first settlers at what is now Tarpon Springs, arrived in 1876 and built a cabin near Spring Bayou; the settlement took the name Tarpon Springs in 1879. In 1880 Hamilton Disston bought four million acres of central west Florida from Florida's governor at 25 cents an acre, opening the area to development.
timeline.notes: spongedocks.net Tarpon Springs History: 'The first settlers... were A.W. Ormond and his daughter, Mary. They arrived in 1876. They built a cabin near Spring Bayou.' 'In 1879, she named the small settlement Tarpon Springs.' Disston: 'bought four million acres of the central west coast of Florida from the Governor for 25 cents an acre' (year 1880 per the page).

timeline.title: Fort Brooke is decommissioned
timeline.text: The Army decommissioned Fort Brooke in 1883, the year before the railroad arrived. Apart from two cannons recovered from the river and displayed on the University of Tampa campus, no trace of the fort remains above ground; artifacts were recovered from the site in the 1970s and 1980s.
timeline.notes: History of Tampa (Wikipedia): 'Fort Brooke was decommissioned in 1883. Except for two cannons fished from the river and displayed on the nearby University of Tampa campus, all traces of the fort are gone.' TBHC exhibit page mentions artifacts recovered from the site during the 1970s and 1980s.

timeline.title: Henry Plant's railroad reaches Tampa
timeline.text: In 1884 Henry B. Plant brought the railroad to Tampa, ending the town's isolation; that year the line also reached the town then called Cork, which incorporated in 1885 as Plant City in his honor. Plant began developing Port Tampa as a deepwater port in 1887, and in 1888 his system finished a nine-mile spur from Tampa to it.
timeline.notes: Plant Museum chronology: '1884 Henry Plant brings the railroad to Tampa'; '1887: Plant begins to develop Port Tampa as a deepwater port'; '1888: Plant System completes a nine-mile railroad spur connecting Tampa to Port Tampa.' Plant City: original name Ichepucksassa, renamed Cork by the postmaster; 'In 1884, Henry B. Plant extended the South Florida Railroad into the town and 1 year later, when the town was incorporated, it was once again renamed this time in honor of Henry B. Plant.' Coordinates: Tampa Union Station (history-of-tampa's anchor for this event); the 1884 depot site is not stated by the source.

timeline.title: Vicente Martínez Ybor agrees to move his cigar business to Tampa
timeline.text: On Oct. 5, 1885, cigar maker Vicente Martínez Ybor contracted with the Tampa Board of Trade to move his hand-rolled cigar business, Ybor & Co., from Key West to Tampa. He bought 40 acres northeast of the town, and work began that October clearing the land for a factory and 50 houses.
timeline.notes: LoC: 'contracted with the Tampa Board of Trade on October 5, 1885, to relocate his hand rolled cigar manufacturing business Ybor & Co.'; 'Ybor purchased 40 acres of land northeast of Tampa'. NHL nomination: 'began developing the land he had purchased near Tampa in October 1885... Workmen felled trees, cleared underbrush... Ybor contracted for a wooden factory and 50 houses'. Coordinates: the Ybor factory, 1916 N 14th St (census).

timeline.title: Ybor City's first cigar factories open
timeline.text: Ignacio Haya's factory went into production first, in March 1886, and Ybor's own factory followed; by the end of 1886 several hundred worker houses stood between today's 6th and 9th avenues and 12th and 14th streets, and more than 3,000 workers had come from Cuba. The 1886 V. M. Ybor factory on 14th Street, the first brick cigar factory built in Tampa, still stands.
timeline.notes: NHL nomination: 'enabled Haya to get into production first, in March 1886'; 'By the end of the year, over 3,000, some 15% of whom were Black, had arrived'; 'By the end of 1886... In the area between present 6th and 9th Avenues and from 12th to 14th Streets, the Ybor and Haya cigar factories were in full operation, several hundred worker houses completed and occupied'. LoC: 'The original building was the first brick cigar factory constructed in Tampa in 1886.'

timeline.title: The Anclote Key lighthouse is built off Tarpon Springs
timeline.text: The Anclote Key Light, a 110-foot cast-iron skeleton tower built to let storm winds and tides blow through, went up on Anclote Key in 1887. It was automated in 1952 and later deactivated; after volunteers had it listed on the National Register in 1999, it was restored and relit on Sept. 13, 2003, and the friends group opens it for climbing on set weekends from October to May.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27 (researcher left it out for lack of a readable page). Friends of Anclote Key State Park & Lighthouse, History page: 'built on Anclote Key as an aid to navigation in 1887. It is 110 feet tall and designed with a skeleton architecture...'; 'In 1952, the lighthouse was automated'; 'placed the lighthouse on the National Register of Historic Places in 1999'; 'restoration was complete in 2003 and the light was relit on September 13, 2003'. Home page: open for climbing the second weekend of each month, Friday-Sunday, 10-4, October-May. Deactivation date differs (Friends: March 4, 1985; Wikipedia: 1984), so it is left out. Point from the history-region place record.

timeline.title: Tarpon Springs becomes Pinellas's first incorporated city
timeline.text: Tarpon Springs incorporated in 1887 with 52 residents, the first incorporated city in what is now Pinellas County. John Cheney, a promoter associated with Hamilton Disston, found that sponges growing in the Gulf could be harvested for money, and in 1890 the Cheney Sponge Company sold almost a million dollars' worth.
timeline.notes: spongedocks.net: 'In 1887, Tarpon Springs was incorporated. It had a population of 52 residents. John Cheney, a promoter associated with Disston, discovered money could be made by harvesting the sponges'; 'By 1890, the sponge industry was firmly established in Tarpon Springs. The Cheney Sponge Company sold almost a million dollars worth of sponges that year.' Pinellas County: 'Tarpon Springs was the first incorporated city in 1887.' Coordinates: 735 Dodecanese Blvd (census), the sponge docks. | Verifier 2026-09-27: removed 'that year' (spongedocks.net gives no year for Cheney's discovery).

timeline.title: Tampa annexes Ybor City
timeline.text: Ybor City's rapid growth led Tampa to annex it in June 1887, although the cigar town kept its own identity; by 1890 it had about 6,000 residents, more than the rest of Tampa. The following month, on July 15, 1887, Tampa organized under a new city charter that also absorbed the Town of North Tampa.
timeline.notes: NHL: 'in June 1887, it became legally part of that city, although it maintained its separate identity... by 1890 it had a population of around 6,000, which outnumbered the native residents of Tampa.' City Clerk: July 15, 1887 charter abolishing the Town of Tampa and Town of North Tampa governments. Coordinates: Ybor City Museum State Park (census, 1818 E 9th Ave).

timeline.title: The Orange Belt Railway reaches St. Petersburg
timeline.text: Peter Demens, an exiled Russian aristocrat, extended his Orange Belt Railroad down the Pinellas peninsula to John C. Williams's settlement in exchange for land, and the first train arrived in 1888 carrying empty freight cars and a single passenger. Legend says the two men flipped a coin to name the town; Demens won and named it for Saint Petersburg, Russia, and Williams named the first hotel the Detroit. Demens built the city's first pier, a railroad pier, in 1889.
timeline.notes: City of St. Petersburg history page (verbatim facts). St. Pete Pier: 'The city's first pier dates back to 1889, built by railroad entrepreneur Peter Demens.' The Dunedin article notes the Orange Belt was the first railroad in Pinellas County (1888); not stated in text.

timeline.title: El Centro Español, Ybor City's first mutual aid society
timeline.text: El Centro Español, founded in 1891, was the first of Ybor City's ethnic mutual aid clubs; members paid dues for social privileges and death and injury benefits. Others followed: L'Unione Italiana (1894), the Deutsch-Amerikanischer Club (1901), Centro Asturiano and El Círculo Cubano (1902) and La Unión Martí-Maceo for Afro-Cubans (1904), Centro Español and Centro Asturiano built their own hospitals, and several of the clubs' clubhouses still stand in Ybor City.
timeline.notes: NHL nomination club table: Centro Asturiano 1902 (building 1913), Circulo Cubano 1902 (1907), Deutsch Amerikanisher 1901, El Centro Espanol 1891 (1912), La Union Marti-Maceo 1904, L'Unione Italiana 1894 (1918); 'El Centro Espanol, the first ethnic club of Tampa'; 'Centro Espanol's Sanatorio, completed in 1906'. NPS lesson 51: 'El Centro Espanol, founded in 1891, was the first mutual aid society in Ybor City... Members paid 25 cents a week to enjoy social privileges as well as death and injury benefits.' The lesson gives 1904 for Centro Asturiano and 1899 for the Cuban club's predecessor; the NHL table years are used. Coordinates: El Centro Español clubhouse, 1536 E 7th Ave (census).

timeline.title: Clear Water Harbor incorporates
timeline.text: The settlement near the Seminole War outpost of Fort Harrison grew after Peter Demens's railroad arrived in 1888, and the town of Clear Water Harbor incorporated in 1891; the name Clearwater came into use in 1906. Dunedin, named by two Scotsmen who applied for its post office, incorporated in 1899.
timeline.notes: Clearwater (Wikipedia): Fort Harrison begun 'around 1835' as a Seminole War outpost; growth prompted by 'Peter Demens' completion of the first passenger railroad line into the city in 1888'; '1891 – Town of Clear Water Harbor incorporated'; 'Prior to 1906, the area was known as Clear Water Harbor.' Dunedin (Wikipedia): 'In 1899, it was incorporated as the Town of Dunedin'. Dunedin: 'Two Scotsmen, J.O. Douglas and James Somerville, later named the settlement Dunedin after applying for the first post office in northern Pinellas County.' City sites myclearwater.com and dunedingov.com returned 403.

timeline.title: Plant opens the Tampa Bay Hotel
timeline.text: Henry Plant opened the Tampa Bay Hotel, a winter resort designed in the style of a Moorish palace beside the Hillsborough River, on Feb. 5, 1891, after building it from 1888. It operated as a hotel until 1932; since 1933 the building has been leased to the University of Tampa, and its south wing is the Henry B. Plant Museum.
timeline.notes: Plant Museum: 'February 5th Tis Done! Plant opens the Tampa Bay Hotel as a winter resort'; 1932 'closes forever as a lavish winter resort hotel'; 1933 'leased to The University of Tampa by the city'. NPS: 'Constructed between 1888 and 1891'; 'operated from 1891 until 1932'; 'The Henry B. Plant Museum in the south wing'. NPS: 'Designed in the style of a Moorish palace'; 'contained over 500 rooms'. | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'on the west bank' is not on the cited pages; the Plant Museum chronology places the casino between the hotel and the river, so 'beside the Hillsborough River'. 1933 lease per NPS.

timeline.title: José Martí rallies Ybor City for Cuban independence
timeline.text: On Nov. 26 and 27, 1891, José Martí gave two speeches in Ybor City, 'With All and For All' and 'The New Growth', that set out the goals of the Cuban Revolutionary Party. In 1893 he spoke from the steps of the V. M. Ybor factory to a crowd of more than 10,000, and afterward workers pledged a day's pay a week to the revolution; the site of the home of Ruperto and Paulina Pedroso, Black Cubans who sheltered him when Spanish assassins came looking for him, is now Parque Amigos de José Martí.
timeline.notes: NPS Teaching with Historic Places lesson 51: 'On November 26 and 27, 1891, he delivered two speeches there—Con Todos Y Para Todos (With All and For All), and Los Pinos Nuevos (The New Growth)—which outlined the goals of the United Cuban Revolutionary Party'; 'In 1893... More than 10,000 Cubans jammed into a small outdoor area in front of the V.M. Ybor Cigar Factory'; 'workers from all the factories pledged to give one day's pay a week'. NHL: 'In 1893 Cuban patriot Jose Marti delivered a speech from the steps' (portico later taken to Havana; present one a reproduction). Pedroso site = Parque Amigos de José Martí at 1300 E. 8th Ave per history-of-tampa's reading of the NHL nomination ('two Black Cubans who sheltered Marti when Spanish assassins were sent'); Coordinates: 1300 E 8th Ave (census).

timeline.title: Hugh Macfarlane founds West Tampa
timeline.text: In 1892 Scottish businessman Hugh Macfarlane founded West Tampa across the Hillsborough River as a second cigar town; by 1900 it was one of the most populous places in Florida, mostly Cuban cigar workers. Together Ybor City and West Tampa made Tampa, in the National Park Service's words, the hand-rolled cigar capital of the world by 1900. Tampa annexed West Tampa in 1925.
timeline.notes: History of Tampa (Wikipedia): 'In 1892, Scottish businessman Hugh MacFarlane founded West Tampa... By 1900, the town already had one of the largest populations in Florida, mostly Cubans involved in the cigar industry'; 'Also in 1925... Tampa annexed the neighboring town of West Tampa.' NHL: 'By 1900 Tampa had become the hand-rolled cigar capital of the world... In addition to Ybor City, another cigar-making community, West Tampa, grew up'.

timeline.title: St. Petersburg incorporates as a town
timeline.text: St. Petersburg incorporated as a town on Feb. 29, 1892, and reincorporated as a city in 1903, when it still had only a few hundred residents.
timeline.notes: City: 'On February 29, 1892 the town of St. Petersburg was incorporated. Then in 1903, with a population of only a few hundred people, St. Petersburg reincorporated as a city.'

timeline.title: Plant opens the Hotel Belleview at Belleair
timeline.text: Henry Plant's Hotel Belleview opened on a bluff at Belleair, south of Clearwater, overlooking Clearwater Bay; the Henry B. Plant Museum's chronology dates the opening to 1897 (Wikipedia gives Jan. 15, 1897), while the hotel's present owner says 1896. Restored as The Belleview Inn, it is, its owner says, the only Plant hotel still operating as a hotel.
timeline.notes: Opal Collection: 'The Belleview Inn (opened in 1896 under the name The Hotel Belleview), which sits on a bluff in Belleair overlooking what is now Clearwater Bay'; 'the only Henry Plant hotel still in operation as a hotel'. Wikipedia Clearwater gives 1897, and Wikipedia Belleview-Biltmore Hotel says it 'was built in the summer of 1896 by railroad tycoon Henry B. Plant and opened January 15, 1897'; the owner's 1896 is kept, attributed, and the discrepancy is noted for the verifier (year 1896 could move to 1897). Coordinates: 25 Belleview Blvd (census). | Verifier 2026-09-27: year changed 1896 -> 1897. The Plant Museum chronology ('1897 Hotel Belleview opens in Belleair'), Wikipedia (opened January 15, 1897) and the Clearwater article (built 1897) agree; only the owner's blog says 1896, now attributed. Id renamed from belleview-hotel-opens-1896 (research only, never published); the media subject was updated.

timeline.title: Tampa becomes the Army's port of embarkation for Cuba
timeline.text: In 1898 the government chose Tampa as the official port of embarkation for the Spanish-American War. About 30,000 soldiers, among them Theodore Roosevelt and his Rough Riders, arrived by late spring and camped in seven army camps, and from May the Tampa Bay Hotel served as headquarters for the officers planning the campaign; the war lasted 10 weeks.
timeline.notes: NPS Tampa Bay Hotel: 'chose Tampa as the official port of embarkation for American forces heading to Cuba'; '30,000 soldiers who arrived in Tampa by the late spring of 1898'; 'seven army camps in the Tampa area'; 'Colonel Roosevelt, and his Rough Riders'; 'headquarters for the Army officers planning the war campaign'; 'The war only lasted 10 weeks'. Plant Museum: 'May, Tampa Bay Hotel becomes headquarters...'. Troops actually loaded at Port Tampa (history-of-tampa note).

timeline.title: Forts rise on Mullet Key and Egmont Key
timeline.text: The Spanish-American War brought coastal forts to the mouth of Tampa Bay: construction of Fort De Soto on Mullet Key began in November 1898 and finished in 1906, and Fort Dade was built on Egmont Key. Fort De Soto was active until 1910; its mortar batteries, placed on the National Register in 1977, stand in today's county park.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia Fort De Soto Park: 'Construction of Fort De Soto began in November 1898 and was completed in 1906'; 'Fort De Soto was active from 1898 to 1910'; named in 1900 for Hernando de Soto; Fort Dade listed in its battery table. Pinellas County: 'The 12-inch mortar battery... was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1977.' Fort Dade on Egmont Key (1898): the egmont-key-state-park record in the outdoors slice ('Fort Dade was built in 1898'). Coordinates: the park (Photon). | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'mortar battery' -> 'batteries' (Batteries Laidley and Bigelow were listed Dec. 2, 1977).

timeline.title: The fair that becomes the Florida State Fair begins in Tampa
timeline.text: The South Florida Fair Association formed in Tampa in 1904 to stage an annual exhibition; it took the name Florida State Fair in 1915 and in 1977 moved to its present grounds at Interstate 4 and U.S. 301 east of the city.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'In 1904, the South Florida Fair Association was formed'; 'The name finally changed to the present Florida State Fair in 1915'; 'By 1977, the first fair was held at its current location, at the intersection of Interstate 4 and U.S. [301]'. floridastatefair.com history URL returned 404.

timeline.title: Ye Mystic Krewe of Gasparilla 'captures' Tampa for the first time
timeline.text: Gasparilla began in 1904 when Tampa Tribune society editor Louise Francis Dodge and George W. Hardee organized a mock pirate attack to promote the city's May Day celebration; the first krewe of about forty rode in on horseback during the parade on May 4, 1904. The krewe first invaded by ship in 1911, and in 1954 it christened the José Gasparilla II, which it calls the only ship built for 'piratical' purposes in two hundred years.
timeline.notes: YMKG: 'Gasparilla began in 1904 when Miss Louise Francis Dodge, society editor of the Tampa Tribune, and George W. Hardee... conspired to promote the City of Tampa and its May Day celebration'; 'the first Ye Mystic Krewe of Gasparilla, whose forty members'; 'arrived on horseback and captured the city during the Festival Parade on May 4, 1904'; 'In 1911 a ship was used for the first time'; José Gasparilla II christened January 5, 1954, 'the only ship that has been constructed for piratical purposes in the past two hundred years' verified in the raw page: 'This is the only ship that has been constructed for piratical purposes in the past two hundred years.' gasparillapiratefest.com history page not opened.

timeline.title: Casimiro Hernandez Sr. opens the Columbia in Ybor City
timeline.text: Spanish-Cuban immigrant Casimiro Hernandez Sr. helped open the Columbia Saloon in Ybor City on Dec. 17, 1903; it became the Columbia Restaurant in 1905 and has since grown to fill an entire city block. The family, now in its fifth generation, calls it Florida's oldest restaurant, and the National Park Service calls it Ybor City's oldest continuously operating eating establishment.
timeline.notes: Columbia site (WebFetch): founded 1905 (as Columbia Saloon in 1903), Casimiro Hernandez, Sr., a Spanish-Cuban immigrant, 'Florida's Oldest Restaurant', fifth-generation family members. NHL: 'Casimirio Hernandez founded it in 1905 as a corner bar and coffee shop... by the 1930s the restaurant had taken on its present dimensions.' NPS place page: 'The oldest continuously operating restaurant in Ybor City'. Place id columbia-restaurant-ybor-city follows SCHEMA.md's example; the eat-tampa slice may use it. Coordinates: 2117 E 7th Ave (census). | Verifier 2026-09-27: the restaurant's page says the Columbia Saloon opened Dec. 17, 1903 and became the Columbia Restaurant in 1905; 'corner bar and coffee shop on 7th Avenue' was not on the cited pages and is removed.

timeline.title: Greek sponge divers transform Tarpon Springs
timeline.text: Experienced divers from Greece came to Tarpon Springs with rubber diving suits and helmets that increased the harvest, and by 1905 more than 500 Greek sponge divers were working from 50 boats. Sponge buyers built the Sponge Exchange in 1907, where catches were stored for auctions twice a week.
timeline.notes: spongedocks.net: 'experienced divers from Greece were brought to Tarpon Springs. By using rubberized diving suits and helmets, they increased harvests. By 1905, over 500 Greek sponge divers were at work using 50 boats.' 'Sponge buyers created the Sponge Exchange in 1907. A building with a courtyard was erected in which each sponger could store his catch while awaiting the auctions that took place twice a week.' Other accounts give 1908 for the exchange; the page's 1907 is used.

timeline.title: Fire destroys 350 buildings in Ybor City
timeline.text: A fire in 1908 destroyed 350 buildings in Ybor City between 16th and 20th streets and 12th and Michigan (now Columbus Drive) avenues. Rebuilding replaced many frame buildings with brick, and into the 1930s owners added the wrought-iron balconies, stucco and Spanish tile that give 7th Avenue its look.
timeline.notes: NHL: 'many frame commercial and commercial-residential buildings were replaced with brick ones, particularly after a disastrous fire in 1908, in which 350 buildings were destroyed in the area between 16th and 20th Streets and 12th and Michigan Avenues (Columbus Drive). Also, during this period, and into the 1930s, many property owners added wrought-iron balconies, stucco, and Spanish tile'.

timeline.title: George Turner Sr. buys the land that becomes Sunken Gardens
timeline.text: The gardens say plumber and gardener George Turner Sr. bought the 4.1 acres in St. Petersburg in 1911; he drained a sinkhole called Curlew Pond with clay tiles, and by the early 1930s neighbors were paying 15 cents to tour his sunken garden. His family ran it as a roadside attraction until selling it to the city in 1999, and it is a local historic landmark.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. Sunken Gardens history timeline: '1911 George Turner Sr., a plumber, avid gardener, and real-estate prospector, purchased the 4.1 acres'; drained 'the sinkhole known as Curlew Pond'; 'by the early 1930's he was charging fifteen cents for tours'; 'designation as a protected Local Historic Landmark in 1998'. Wikipedia gives 1903 and six acres for the purchase (attributed year kept to the gardens' own page) and says the family sold it to the city in 1999.

timeline.title: The Jackson House takes in Black travelers by Union Station
timeline.text: Moses and Sarah Jackson built a house less than a block from the future Tampa Union Station in the late 1890s and turned it into a boarding house, perhaps as early as 1910; it grew after the station opened in 1912, lodging African American railroad workers and visitors while Black travelers were barred from white hotels into the early 1960s. The city says it is the only such boarding house in Tampa still standing.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. City Soulwalk marker: 'originally constructed as a private residence by Moses and Sarah Jackson in the late 1890s'; 'That conversion may have begun as early as 1910, but the house grew in importance and in physical size after the opening of Tampa Union Station'; 'less than one block to the east'; 'through the early 1960s, African Americans were prohibited from staying in white hotels, motels, and boarding houses'; 'it is the only one that remains standing'. Year 1912 = Union Station's opening, which the marker ties the boarding house's growth to.

timeline.title: Pinellas County splits from Hillsborough
timeline.text: After a local referendum in favor of separation from Hillsborough County, Pinellas became Florida's 48th county on Jan. 1, 1912. Its name comes from the Spanish Punta Pinal, 'point of pines'.
timeline.notes: Pinellas County: 'Pinellas became the state's 48th county on January 1, 1912, after a local referendum passed calling for separation from Hillsborough County.' 'Pinellas is derived from the Spanish words Punta Pinal meaning point of pines.'

timeline.title: Tampa Union Station opens
timeline.text: Tampa Union Station opened on May 15, 1912. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974, closed in 1984 and reopened in 1998 after restoration; Amtrak trains still use it.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'opened on May 15, 1912, by the Tampa Union Station Company'; 'Built in 1912, it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1974... closed in 1984 and reopened in 1998 after restoration'; Amtrak platform works 2020. timeline.title: Big-league spring training comes to St. Petersburg
timeline.text: In 1914 former mayor Al Lang persuaded Branch Rickey to bring the St. Louis Browns to St. Petersburg for spring training, the start of the city's spring-training history; the waterfront ballpark built in 1947 and named for Lang, Al Lang Stadium, has been the Tampa Bay Rowdies' home since 2011. The city's first library opened on Mirror Lake in December 1915.
timeline.notes: City: 'In 1914, the rich history of spring training and Florida's love affair with baseball began when the city's former mayor, Al Lang, convinced Branch Rickey to move his St. Louis Browns to the Sunshine City for spring training.' 'the city's first library was built along Mirror Lake, opening its doors in December of 1915.' Al Lang Stadium as the Rowdies' home since 2011: venues-bay slice record al-lang-stadium (source rowdiessoccer.com). | Verifier 2026-09-27: the Rowdies clause was unsourced; now cited to the club's Al Lang Stadium page (built 1947, named for Lang, Rowdies' home since the 2011 season).

timeline.title: The St. Petersburg-Tampa Airboat Line starts scheduled flights
timeline.text: On Jan. 1, 1914, pilot Tony Jannus flew former St. Petersburg mayor Abram C. Pheil, who had bought the first ticket at auction for $400, across the bay to Tampa in a Benoist flying boat, the first flight of the St. Petersburg-Tampa Airboat Line, organized by Percival Fansler. The City of Tampa calls it the world's first scheduled commercial airline service; the line flew until May 1914.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia SPT Airboat Line: 'On January 1, 1914, the SPT Airboat Line became the first scheduled winged airline service in the United States'; in service January to May 1914 (ceased May 5, 1914); Fansler brought in Thomas Benoist; 'It was won with a final bid of $400 by the former mayor of St. Petersburg, Abram C. Pheil'; 23-minute flight. tampa.gov: 'In 1914 Percival Ellicott Fansler introduced the world's first scheduled commercial airline service'. Pilot Tony Jannus: History of Tampa (Wikipedia).

timeline.title: The 1921 hurricane floods Bayshore and strikes Tarpon Springs
timeline.text: Late on Oct. 25, 1921, a major hurricane made landfall near Tarpon Springs, the first major hurricane to hit the Tampa Bay area since 1848. Storm surge flooded Tampa's Ballast Point, Hyde Park, Palmetto Beach and other neighborhoods around Bayshore Boulevard, the storm left at least eight deaths, four of them in Tampa, and it cut Hurricane Pass through Hog Island, splitting it into today's Honeymoon and Caladesi islands.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'making landfall near Tarpon Springs, Florida, late on October 25'; 'the first to do so there since the hurricane of 1848'; 'Several neighborhoods in Tampa were inundated, especially the interbay neighborhoods of Ballast Point, DeSoto Park, Edgewater Park, Hyde Park, Palmetto Beach, and other areas in the vicinity of Bayshore Boulevard'; 'Four deaths occurred in Tampa'; 'the hurricane left at least eight deaths'. No NWS page could be reached (weather.gov/tbw URLs tried returned 404). Coordinates: Bayshore Boulevard (see-tampa slice point). | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'the first to strike' corrected to 'the first major hurricane to hit ... since 1848' (the article's words); added Hurricane Pass from the Honeymoon Island State Park article.

timeline.title: A Smithsonian dig at Weedon Island names a culture
timeline.text: Smithsonian Institution archaeologist J. Walter Fewkes excavated a mound on Weedon Island in Old Tampa Bay in 1923 and 1924, and the decorated ceremonial pottery first described there gave its name to the Weeden Island culture of the Southeast. The island, later home to homesteaders, speakeasies, a Hollywood movie studio and a 1930s airport, is now Pinellas County's Weedon Island Preserve.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia Weeden Island culture: 'The site on Weedon Island where Weeden Island sacred ceramics were first described was excavated by Smithsonian Institution archaeologist J. Walter Fewkes in 1923 and 1924'; name 'derived from the Weedon Island site (despite the dissimilar spellings) in Old Tampa Bay in Pinellas County'. Preserve history page: 'homesteaders, speakeasies, a Hollywood movie studio and a 1930s airport'. Coordinates: Photon nature_reserve match.

timeline.title: The Gandy Bridge links Tampa and St. Petersburg
timeline.text: George S. Gandy's toll bridge across Old Tampa Bay opened on Nov. 20, 1924; at two and a half miles it was then the longest automobile toll bridge in the world. The City of St. Petersburg says it cut travel time to Tampa by more than half. The original span was dismantled in 1975 and the route is now carried by newer Gandy bridges.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia Gandy Bridge: 'Construction began in September 1922 and the bridge was completed for a formal opening on November 20, 1924'; 'spanned a distance of two and a half miles, making it the longest automobile toll bridge in the world at that time'; 'The original 1924 span was dismantled in 1975.' City: 'In 1924 the Gandy Bridge opened—cutting travel time to Tampa by more than half'. Area: the bridge crosses between South Tampa and NE St. Pete; area set to northeast-stpete (Gandy Beach is listed under that area in SPEC §4.1).

timeline.title: Elder Jordan builds the hall that becomes the Manhattan Casino
timeline.text: In 1925 Black entrepreneur Elder Jordan contracted with R. L. Sharpe to build a 12,000-square-foot, two-story entertainment hall on 22nd Street South in St. Petersburg; it opened as the Jordan Dance Hall in 1931 and, as the Manhattan Casino, drew leading Black musicians and later rock and roll and blues singers. It closed in 1968 and has since been revived as an event hall.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. City page: 'In 1925, a local African-American entrepreneur named Elder Jordan contracted with R.L. Sharpe to build a 12,000 sq. ft. two-story entertainment facility, which first opened as the Jordan Dance Hall in 1931'; big bands, then rock and roll and blues in the 1960s; 'The venue closed its doors in 1968 but has been revived in recent years as an events hall'. timeline.title: The Vinoy Park Hotel opens on New Year's Eve
timeline.text: Aymer Vinoy Laughner's 375-room hotel on the St. Petersburg waterfront, designed by Henry L. Taylor, went up in just under 10 months from Feb. 5, 1925, and opened on New Year's Eve 1925. It became an Army Air Forces and Maritime Service training center in 1942, closed in 1974 and reopened in 1992 after restoration; it operates today as The Vinoy Resort & Golf Club.

Miller, 'the 375-room hotel in just under 10 months, in time for a grand opening on New Year's Eve 1925'; 'On July 3, 1942, The Vinoy ceased operation as a hotel and was leased to the U.S. Army Air Force and subsequently the United States Maritime Service as a training center'; 'In 1974, the hotel closed its doors for good'; 'in 1992, The Vinoy reopened as a Stouffer Hotel.' Name of the current operation: stays-stpete-pinellas slice id vinoy-resort-golf-club. Coordinates from that slice.

timeline.title: A causeway opens Madeira Beach to homes
timeline.text: Madeira Beach's shape comes from the hurricane of 1848, which cut the inlet named John's Pass for early homesteader John (Juan) Levique. Attempts to settle the island failed until 1926, when a causeway from the mainland let the first houses go up; a bridge across John's Pass followed a year later.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27 (Gulf Beaches had only five records). Madeira Beach article: 'The modern shape of Madeira Beach was formed by a hurricane, the "Gale of '48", carving out the strait now known as John's Pass. The new waterway was named after an early homesteader, John (Juan) Levique. Several aborted attempts to settle the area occurred in the early 1900s, but it was not until 1926 that a causeway was built between the mainland and Madeira Beach, allowing for the first houses to be constructed in the area. A bridge was built crossing John's Pass a year later.' Point from the johns-pass-village place record.

timeline.title: The Florida land boom breaks in Tampa
timeline.text: Tampa's real-estate boom peaked in 1925, with new subdivisions such as Davis Islands, Palma Ceia and Seminole Heights, and began to break in 1926 when financial backing for Davis Islands collapsed. Developer D. P. Davis, who had built the islands from mud dredged from the bay, was lost at sea that October, and by the winter of 1926-27 the market had reached saturation.

Beach Park, Davis Islands, Palma Ceia, Sunset Park, and Seminole Heights. During 1925, the Florida boom was in its heyday'; 'Early signs of an economic slow-down in Tampa were evident in 1926 with the collapse of financial backing for the Davis Islands real estate venture. By the winter of 1926-27 the saturation point for real estate development had finally been reached.' timeline.title: St. Petersburg opens the Million Dollar Pier
timeline.text: The Million Dollar Pier, with its casino, opened in 1926 and quickly became one of St. Petersburg's main gathering places. It followed the 1889 Railroad Pier, the Electric Pier of 1906 and the 1913 Municipal Recreation Pier, the city's first built for automobiles.
timeline.notes: St. Pete Pier history: 1889 Railroad Pier (Peter Demens); 1906 Electric Pier; 'Opened in 1913, the Municipal Recreation Pier was St. Petersburg's first automobile-friendly pier'; 'Opened in 1926, the Million Dollar Pier (and its casino) quickly became one of St. Petersburg's premier gathering places.' Coordinates: the St. Pete Pier (see-pinellas slice point).

timeline.title: Tampa Downs opens for Thoroughbred racing
timeline.text: Horse racing came to the top of the bay when Tampa Downs opened on Feb. 18, 1926, with Babe Ruth, Jack Dempsey, Gene Sarazen and John Ringling at the first card. The Army took over the track in 1943 for jungle-warfare training; renamed Sunshine Park in 1946 and later also known as Florida Downs, it races today as Tampa Bay Downs.

Opening under the name Tampa Downs on Feb. 18, the inaugural card featured appearances by sports legends Babe Ruth, heavyweight boxer Jack Dempsey and golfer Gene Sarazen and circus impresario John Ringling'; 'Army took over the track in 1943 for use as a jungle-warfare training facility'; Sunshine Park Racing Association.
