timeline.title: Tampa Theatre opens on Franklin Street
timeline.text: John Eberson's atmospheric movie palace opened on Franklin Street on Oct. 15, 1926, and was the city's first commercial building with air conditioning. Threatened with demolition in 1973, it was rescued when the City of Tampa stepped in; it reopened in early 1978, the year it was listed on the National Register, and still shows films in a 1,238-seat auditorium.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'Designed as an atmospheric theatre-style movie palace by architect John Eberson, it opened on October 15, 1926'; 'In 1973, the theatre faced the same fate'; 'By the time it reopened in early 1978'; NRHP 1978. Hillsborough County marker page: 'When Tampa Theatre opened in 1926 it was the city's first commercial building to offer air conditioning'; 'the City of Tampa rescued the theater'; 1,238 seats; county page raw text: 'Today, the 1,238-seat theater is thriving' (Wikipedia gives 1,252 after the 2017 renovation; the county figure is used). tampatheatre.org serves a bot challenge (HTTP 202) and could not be read.

timeline.title: The Don CeSar opens on St. Pete Beach
timeline.text: Thomas Rowe opened the Don CeSar on St. Pete Beach in 1928; the hotel calls itself the Pink Palace. The Army bought it in 1942 for use as a hospital and then a convalescent center for airmen, and after the war it housed Veterans Administration offices until 1969; saved by a citizens' group, it was restored and reopened as a resort in 1973.
timeline.notes: Don CeSar history page: 1928 'Real estate scion Thomas Rowe opens The Don CeSar on St. Pete Beach'; 1942 'The U.S. Army purchases the hotel to be used as a sub-base hospital, then a convalescent center for airmen'; VA headquarters until 1969; citizens' group 1971; Bowman restoration 1972; 'reopens as a full-service resort' 1973. Raw page: 'The Legendary Pink Palace'; 'Opened in the heyday of the Gatsby Era in 1928'. Hurricane status 2024-26: see the stays-beaches slice.

timeline.title: President Coolidge dedicates Bok Tower
timeline.text: On Feb. 1, 1929, President Calvin Coolidge dedicated Edward Bok's Singing Tower and its surrounding sanctuary near Lake Wales, a carillon tower designed by Milton B. Medary set in gardens by Frederick Law Olmsted Jr. Bok Tower Gardens is a National Historic Landmark.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'Outgoing President Calvin Coolidge dedicated the tower on February 1, 1929'; the dedication inscription; 'Bok Tower Gardens is a National Historic Landmark'; Medary designed the tower. Olmsted Jr. named on the official history page's menu ('Olmsted Gardens & Trails') and the around-daytrips heritage block; the official page's text did not render dates in a raw read.

timeline.title: One of Tampa's largest banks fails ahead of the crash
timeline.text: The collapse of the Citizens Bank and Trust Company, one of Tampa's largest banks, on July 17, 1929, set off runs on the Bank of Ybor and other local banks months before the October stock market crash. Winter visitors stayed home, firms laid off workers and building stopped as the Depression began.
timeline.notes: North Franklin Street HD NRHP form: 'the collapse of one of the city's largest banks, the Citizens Bank and Trust Company on July 17, 1929 was the precursor of a financial crisis to come. A run on Tampa's banks including the Bank of Ybor, Franklin Bank... This was followed by the stock market crash in October 1929. Thousands of winter visitors remained in their northern homes. Hundreds of firms laid off employees. Building activities ceased.'

timeline.title: The Ringling Museum of Art opens in Sarasota
timeline.text: Circus owner John Ringling and his wife Mable finished their Sarasota mansion, Ca' d'Zan, in 1926, moved the circus's winter quarters to Sarasota in 1927, and opened the John and Mable Ringling Museum of Art to the public in 1930. On his death in 1936 Ringling left the museum and estate to the people of Florida; the state took control in 1946, and Florida State University has governed it since 2000.
timeline.notes: The Ringling (raw page text): Ca' d'Zan 'completed in 1926 after only two years of construction'; 'In 1927, John moved the winter quarters of the circus from Bridgeport, Connecticut to Sarasota'; 'The John and Mable Ringling Museum of Art opened to the public in 1930'; 'upon his own death in 1936, John bequeathed the museum and the rest of his estate to the people of Florida'; 'When the state prevailed and took control in 1946'; 'In 2000... the state transferred governance of the museum to Florida State University'.

timeline.title: Plant City holds the first Strawberry Festival
timeline.text: Members of the newly organized Plant City Lions Club started the Florida Strawberry Festival in 1930 to celebrate the strawberry harvest. It paused for six years during and after World War II and was revived in 1948; the city says more than three-quarters of the nation's midwinter strawberries come from Plant City.
timeline.notes: Festival history: 'The event began back in 1930 when members of the newly organized Plant City Lions Club conceived the idea of an event to celebrate the bountiful harvest of strawberries'; 'a six-year hiatus during and immediately following World War II'; reactivated 1948 with American Legion Post 26. City: 'over 3/4 of the nation's midwinter strawberries come from Plant City'.

timeline.title: A cigar strike ends the reign of the lectores
timeline.text: After a major cigarworkers' strike in 1931, Ybor City's factory owners brought in lower-paid workers and removed the lectores, the readers hired to read aloud to the cigar rollers as they worked. Cigarettes, cigar-making machines and the Depression hit the hand-rolled industry hard; between 1930 and 1940 a quarter of Tampa's foreign-born whites and more than half of its Afro-Cubans left the city.
timeline.notes: NHL: 'A major strike by cigarworkers in 1931 also contributed to change in Ybor City. The owners brought in many lower-paid native workers and removed the lectores from the factories'; 'The combined effects of the spit campaign, the Great Depression, and the popularity of cigarettes dealt Ybor City's hand-rolled cigar industry a blow from which it never recovered'; 'Between 1930 and 1940, one-quarter of the foreign-born whites, and more than one-half of the Afro-Cubans, left Tampa.' NHL: 'lectores (readers) hired to entertain workers used patriotic texts'.

timeline.title: The Davis Causeway links Tampa and Clearwater
timeline.text: Ben T. Davis began building a causeway across Old Tampa Bay between Tampa and Clearwater in 1927; stalled by the bust and the Depression, it opened in 1934 at a cost of $900,000, with a toll of 25 cents a car. Today it is the Courtney Campbell Causeway, carrying State Road 60.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia Courtney Campbell Causeway: 'work began in earnest in 1927'; 'Costing $900,000 in total, the Davis Causeway was opened on January 28, 1934, with a 25¢ toll per car' in the text, but its infobox and the History of Tampa article say June 28, 1934; only the year is given here. History of Tampa: builder Ben T. Davis; construction halted by the crash of the land boom and the Depression; RFC loan 1933.

timeline.title: The CCC builds one of Florida's first state parks
timeline.text: Hillsborough River State Park, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps, was one of the eight original Florida state parks created in 1938. CCC buildings, a suspension bridge and a section of fence survive on a stretch of river known for small rapids, and the park's interpretive center tells the story of Fort Foster across the road.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'one of the eight original Florida State Parks created in 1938'; 'originally built by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), and some of the original structures remain, including the buildings that now house the administrative offices and Interpretive Center, the suspension bridge, and a section of fence'. Infobox 'established = 1935'. Wikipedia: 'This section of the river is noted for having several clusters of small rapids'. Preservation Society: the Interpretive Center 'hosts over 100 artifacts that were found at the Fort Foster Historic Site'. floridastateparks.org returns 403.

timeline.title: Frank Lloyd Wright begins his Florida Southern campus
timeline.text: Frank Lloyd Wright first walked the Florida Southern College campus in Lakeland on May 8, 1938, at the invitation of president Ludd Spivey. Over more than 20 years he produced 18 designs, 13 of which were built, starting with the chapel (1938-41); the college calls it the world's largest single-site collection of Wright's architecture for one client.
timeline.notes: Florida Southern: 'On May 8, 1938, at nearly 71 years of age, Wright set foot on the Florida Southern campus for the first time'; 'he delivered 18 unique and distinctive building designs over the course of more than 20 years'; 'Thirteen of his proposed structures were funded and built'; 'This easily makes Florida Southern the world's largest single-site collection of Wright's architecture for one client'; 'Construction of the chapel lasted from 1938 to 1941.'

timeline.title: The Army builds MacDill Field on Catfish Point
timeline.text: The Army established Southeast Air Base, Tampa, on Catfish Point in 1939, named it MacDill Field for Col. Leslie MacDill and dedicated it on April 16, 1941. MacDill and Drew Field, the city airport the Army leased in 1940, drew tens of thousands of soldiers and workers, and by war's end 25,000 soldiers had been trained locally to crew B-17 and B-29 bombers.
timeline.notes: MacDill AFB (Wikipedia): 'originally established in 1939 as Southeast Air Base, Tampa'; 'named in honor of Colonel Leslie MacDill (1889–1938)'. History of Tampa: base announced July 15, 1939 at Catfish Point; named MacDill Field on November 30; 'MacDill Field would be dedicated on April 16, 1941.' TPA (Wikipedia): 'In 1940, the City of Tampa leased Drew Field to the U.S. [Army]'. North Franklin NRHP form: 'Tens of thousands of soldiers and workers supported the war effort at Tampa's revitalized shipyards and at MacDill and Drew Fields... By war's end, 25,000 soldiers had been trained locally to man the nation's B-17 and B-29 bomber fleets.' 'Interbay Peninsula' tip: base location (Photon); macdill.af.mil returned 403.

timeline.title: Honeymoon Island's cottages welcome their first couple
timeline.text: In 1939 New York advertising executive Clinton M. Washburn bought the northern half of Hog Island off Dunedin, built about 50 palm-thatched cottages and promoted it as a honeymoon retreat; the resort opened on March 8, 1940, and a Life magazine feature that April drew couples to a contest for two-week stays. The state acquired the island in 1974 and opened it as a state park in 1981.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. Wikipedia: 'In 1939 the New York advertising executive Clinton M. Washburn purchased the northern half of the former Hog Island'; 'roughly 50 palm-thatched cottages'; 'The resort opened to the public on March 8, 1940'; 'promoted through a Life magazine feature on April 8, 1940'; 'acquired by the state in 1974 and formally opened on December 7, 1981'. floridastateparks.org returns 403. Point from the outdoors place record.

timeline.title: Shipyards and hotels go to war
timeline.text: During World War II the Tampa Shipbuilding and Engineering Company and the Hooker's Point Shipyard built ships for the war effort, and Tampa's shipyard workforce reached 16,000. Across the bay St. Petersburg became a major technical training center for the Army Air Corps: more than 100,000 trainees filled the city's hotels, the Vinoy became a training center in July 1942, and the Army turned the Don CeSar into a hospital.
timeline.notes: Museum of Florida History: 'Florida shipyards included the Tampa Shipbuilding and Engineering Company (later known as TASCO), the Hooker's Point Shipyard in Tampa'. NRHP North Franklin: 'The personnel at Tampa shipyards reached 16,000'. City of St. Petersburg: 'St. Pete became a major technical services training center for the Army Air Corps. More than 100,000 trainees filled every hotel in the city'. Vinoy: leased July 3, 1942. Don CeSar: Army purchase 1942, hospital. Coordinates: Hooker's Point yard (Photon railway yard name 'Hookers Point Yard'); area: Hooker's Point is the port peninsula by the Channel District.

timeline.title: Drew Field returns to the city and becomes Tampa International
timeline.text: The city completed Drew Field, six miles west of downtown, in 1928 and leased it to the Army in 1940. On March 1, 1946, the federal government returned it to the city; Eastern and National airlines moved there from Peter O. Knight Airport on Davis Islands, which was too small for the new prop-liners, and on Oct. 15, 1947, it was renamed Tampa International Airport.
timeline.notes: TPA (Wikipedia): 'In 1928, the city completed the 160 acre Drew Field'; 'In 1940, the City of Tampa leased Drew Field to the U.S. [Army]'. History of Tampa: 'on March 1, 1946, the federal government would give it to the municipal government'; 'The airport would start seeing its first airlines in it during April and May. Drew Field would be renamed on October 15, 1947, to Tampa International Airport.' tampaairport.com returned 403. | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'airlines began flying from it that spring' was not in the sources; replaced with the airport article's account of Eastern and National moving from Peter O. Knight Airport.

timeline.title: Tampa's last streetcar goes to the barn
timeline.text: Tampa's street railway began with steam cars to Ybor City by 1886, went electric in 1893 and at its peak ran on more than 53 miles of track. By the end of World War II only Tampa and St. Petersburg still had streetcars in Florida, and on Aug. 4, 1946, the last Tampa Electric Birney car retired to its carbarn in Tampa Heights.
timeline.notes: TBHC blog (Rodney Kite-Powell): steam street railway between Tampa and Ybor City by 1886; electric in 1893; 'over 53 miles of tracks'; 'By the end of World War II, Tampa and St. Petersburg were the only Florida cities with streetcars'; 'the last Tampa Electric Birney car retired to its carbarn on 7th Avenue in Tampa Heights' on August 4, 1946. The see-tampa slice identifies Armature Works (1910) as Tampa Electric's former streetcar warehouse, but this page does not name the carbarn, so no place link or coordinates are given.

timeline.title: The Phillies begin spring training in Clearwater
timeline.text: The Philadelphia Phillies have trained in Clearwater since 1947, which the team says is the second-longest affiliation between a major league club and its spring training home. They have played spring games at BayCare Ballpark since it opened in 2004.
timeline.notes: MLB Phillies page: 'The Phillies have been training in Clearwater, Florida, since 1947, the second-longest affiliation between a major league club and its spring training home in baseball.' 'BayCare Ballpark opened in 2004 and is the home of Phillies Spring Training'. Coordinates: 601 N Old Coachman Rd (census).

timeline.title: Newt Perry opens Weeki Wachee's mermaid show
timeline.text: In 1947 stunt swimmer and promoter Newt Perry created the Weeki Wachee attraction, building a theater into the limestone of the spring with windows below the water so visitors could watch 'mermaids' perform. It is now Weeki Wachee Springs State Park.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'The attraction was created in 1947 by stunt swimmer and attraction promoter Newt Perry'; 'First an 18-seat theater... were embedded in the lime rock of the spring with viewing windows below the surface of the water'; 'Officially: Weeki Wachee Springs State Park'. floridastateparks.org returns 403.

timeline.title: The Spanish landing and a temple mound are set aside for visitors
timeline.text: In 1948 Congress authorized De Soto National Memorial, where the Manatee River meets Tampa Bay, to commemorate the 1539 expedition. The same year Madira and Karl Bickel donated the land around the temple mound on Terra Ceia Island to the state; it was the first Native American site in Florida designated a State Archaeological Site. Pinellas County also bought back Mullet Key in 1948, the land that became Fort De Soto Park.
timeline.notes: NPS basicinfo: 'Created in 1948, the park's mission is to commemorate the 1539 expedition'. Wikipedia De Soto National Memorial: 'authorized by Congress on March 11, 1948'; the site lies 'where the Manatee River joins Tampa Bay'. Madira Bickel (Wikipedia): 'She and her husband, Karl, purchased the land around the main mound and donated it to the state in 1948'; 'the first Native American location in Florida to be designated as a State Archaeological Site'; established March 16, 1949. Pinellas County: 'The property was repurchased from the United States in 1948 for $26,500.' | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'it became a state park in 1949' is not on the cited pages and is removed.

timeline.title: The first Sunshine Skyway opens across the mouth of the bay
timeline.text: The original Sunshine Skyway, a two-lane bridge across Lower Tampa Bay from St. Petersburg to Terra Ceia in Manatee County, opened to traffic on Sept. 6, 1954. A second two-lane span opened beside it in 1971.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'The two-lane bridge opened to traffic on September 6, 1954'; 'a second two-lane span opened in 1971'; 'Opening of the newer span was delayed until 1971'. Place skyway-fishing-pier-state-park (outdoors slice): the piers are remnants of the old bridges (per that slice; not stated in this source). Area: the bridge spans Pinellas and Manatee; bradenton-anna-maria chosen for the southern approach. FDOT pages not reached. | Verifier 2026-09-27: linked the see-pinellas sunshine-skyway-bridge place and used its point and area (south-stpete) so the bridge and its history sit on the same sheet; the old bridge's remains are Skyway Fishing Pier State Park.

timeline.title: The University of South Florida gets its site
timeline.text: A 1955 state law created a new state university in Hillsborough County, and on Dec. 18, 1956, the Florida Cabinet approved building it on a Fowler Avenue property where a private airport occupied what had been the Hillsborough Army Airfield in World War II; the campus rose on the practice bombing range just north of the airfield. The University of South Florida held its first classes on Sept. 26, 1960, and describes itself as the first major state university planned, built and opened in the 20th century.
timeline.notes: USF history: June 18, 1955, Gov. LeRoy Collins signs House Bill 1007 creating a new state university in Hillsborough County; 'December 18, 1956' Cabinet approves the site, 'the former Hillsborough Army Airfield property on Fowler Avenue'; first classes September 26, 1960; 'the first major state university planned, built and opened in the 20th century'. Raw page: 'USF becomes the first major state university planned, built and opened in the 20th century, as well as Florida's first university located in a major metropolitan area.' | Verifier 2026-09-27: the site was not 'the former Hillsborough Army Airfield' itself; USF's history page says the campus was built on the bombing range just north of it.

timeline.title: Tampa's zoo moves to Lowry Park
timeline.text: Tampa's zoo began as a small animal exhibit in Plant Park on the University of Tampa grounds in the 1930s and moved to its present site in 1957 as the Lowry Park Zoo. It was rebuilt in 1987-1988 and renamed ZooTampa at Lowry Park in 2018.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. Wikipedia: 'ZooTampa traces its origins to a small animal exhibit that was located on the campus of the University of Tampa in downtown beginning in the 1930s. It moved to its current location ... in 1957 and became known as the Lowry Park Zoo'; 'completely redesigned and rebuilt in 1987-1988'; 'In 2018, the zoo was rebranded as "ZooTampa at Lowry Park"'; 'Tampa's first zoo was a small collection of exotic animals in Plant Park'. History of Tampa: 'Lowry Park Zoo opened in 1957.' Point from the see-tampa place record.

timeline.title: Pass-a-Grille and its neighbors become St. Petersburg Beach
timeline.text: In 1957 the towns of Pass-a-Grille, Don CeSar, Belle Vista and St. Petersburg Beach and nearby unincorporated land consolidated as the City of St. Petersburg Beach; voters shortened the name to St. Pete Beach in 1994. Pass-a-Grille was recognized as a National Register historic district in 1989.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. City of St. Pete Beach: 'The city was incorporated in 1957 with the consolidation of the Towns of Pass-a-Grille, Don CeSar, Belle Vista, St. Petersburg Beach and unincorporated Pinellas County to become the "City of St. Petersburg Beach." In 1994, the citizens voted to shorten the name to "St. Pete Beach"'. Pass-a-Grille article: 'in 1989 Pass-a-Grille was recognized as a National Register Historic District'. No point: a city-wide event.

timeline.title: Busch Gardens opens beside Anheuser-Busch's new Tampa brewery
timeline.text: Anheuser-Busch bought 160 acres in Tampa in 1957 for a brewery, and in 1959 it opened Busch Gardens beside it, with gardens, free admission and free beer samples; general admission was first charged in 1970. It has grown into the Busch Gardens Tampa Bay theme park.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'Anheuser-Busch made public on July 25, that it had purchased a 160 acre plot of land in Tampa for $320,000' (1957 section); 'the park opened on March 31, 1959' in the lead but 'The brewery and gardens officially opened to the public for tours on June 1, 1959, as an admission-free facility'; 'Hospitality House'... 'offered free samples of beer'. Because of the two dates only the year is given. History of Tampa: 'Busch Gardens theme park opened in 1959.' buschgardens.com not reached. | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'brewery tours and a hospitality house' not found in the article; replaced by what it states (free samples, free admission until July 31, 1970).

timeline.title: Homes in the Scrub are razed for a housing project
timeline.text: The Scrub, northeast of downtown, grew from a settlement of freed people after the Civil War into Tampa's oldest and largest African American neighborhood, with Central Avenue as its business heart. In 1959 its homes were demolished for the Central Park Village housing project, and in the 1960s construction of I-4 and urban renewal disrupted Central Avenue's businesses.
timeline.notes: City of Tampa Soulwalk marker: 'The Scrub, once Tampa's oldest and largest African American neighborhood'; freed people settled a 'scrub palmetto thicket' after the Civil War; population quadrupled 1900-1930 (4,382 to 21,551); housing demolished 1959 for Central Park Village; 'Construction of I-4 and the Urban Renewal projects in the 1960s disrupted business along Central Avenue'; The Ella opened December 2012 (Encore). Coordinates: history-of-tampa's point for the Scrub clearance (27.9556, -82.4555); area: the Scrub lies just north of downtown (Encore), closest area downtown-tampa.

timeline.title: The Deuces thrives on 22nd Street South
timeline.text: Through the 1940s, '50s and '60s, 22nd Street South in St. Petersburg, known as The Deuces, was a thriving downtown for African American residents, home to the Manhattan Casino, which drew leading Black musicians. The city says it peaked in the 1960s with more than 100 Black-owned or operated businesses, entertainment spots and professional offices; the city's African American Heritage Trail walking tours begin at the Woodson museum at 2240 9th Ave. S.
timeline.notes: City of St. Petersburg: 'Through the 40s, 50s, and 60s, one such neighborhood in South St. Pete became known as The Deuces and developed into a thriving downtown area for African Americans and other minority communities. Home to the iconic Manhattan Casino, which drew America's finest African American musicians, the Deuces reached its peak in the 1960s with more than 100 Black-owned or operated businesses, entertainment spots, and professional offices'. Year 1960 stands for 'the 1960s' (no single-year event); date left empty. '22nd Street South' from the see-pinellas deuces-live record (source deuceslive.org/our-history), not the city page. Coordinates: deuces-live (see-pinellas). | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'the Woodson museum is nearby' replaced by the city's statement that both heritage trails begin at the museum at 2240 9th Ave South.

timeline.title: Students sit in at the Woolworth lunch counter
timeline.text: On Feb. 29, 1960, about 40 students from Middleton and Blake high schools, led by Clarence Fort and the Rev. A. Leon Lowry, staged a peaceful sit-in at the F. W. Woolworth lunch counter at 901 N. Franklin St. By September 1960 Tampa's lunch counters were integrated without the violence seen in many other places.
timeline.notes: City of Tampa Soulwalk marker (verbatim facts). Coordinates: 901 N Franklin St (census).

timeline.title: Fort De Soto Park opens
timeline.text: After the Pinellas Bayway toll road reached Mullet Key in 1962 and let visitors drive to the islands, Fort De Soto Park opened on Dec. 21, 1962, and was dedicated on May 11, 1963. The county park now covers several keys, beaches and the 1898 fort.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'In 1962, a toll road, the Pinellas Bayway... was completed to the mainland, enabling island visitors to arrive by car'; 'On December 21, 1962, Fort De Soto Park opened'; 'On May 11, 1963, Fort De Soto Park was officially dedicated'; park keys: Madelaine Key, St. Jean Key, St. Christopher Key, Bonne Fortune Key and Mullet Key. 'covers several keys' is our summary.

timeline.title: St. Petersburg's Museum of Fine Arts opens
timeline.text: Collector Margaret Acheson Stuart founded the Museum of Fine Arts on the St. Petersburg waterfront, and it opened to the public in 1965; the museum says it was the city's first art museum.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. MFA About page: 'founded by Margaret Acheson Stuart (1896-1980)'; 'The MFA, a city landmark, opened to the public in 1965 - the first art museum in St. Petersburg'. Point from the see-pinellas place record.

timeline.title: Urban renewal and I-4 cut through Ybor City
timeline.text: In 1965 Ybor City became the target of a major urban renewal project: over the next few years 70 acres, including 660 frame houses, two ethnic club buildings, a fire station and a cigarmakers' school, were leveled, and the promised redevelopment largely never came. Construction of Interstate 4 also split the community, but the losses spurred Tampa's Latin community to preserve its culture and landmark buildings.
timeline.notes: NHL: 'In 1965 Ybor City became the target of a major urban renewal project. During the next few years, 70 acres, including 660 frame houses, two ethnic club buildings, a fire station, and a cigarmakers' school were leveled. Although plans for redevelopment were announced, they largely came to naught because expected Federal urban renewal money did not materialize. The construction of Interstate 4 also split the community.' 'the renewal project sparked a revival of interest in the area among the Latin community to preserve its culture and most significant buildings.'

timeline.title: Unrest in Central Park after a police shooting
timeline.text: On June 11, 1967, a Tampa police officer fatally shot Martin Chambers, a 19-year-old unarmed Black man fleeing a burglary, and days of unrest followed in the Central Park neighborhood until June 15. The City of Tampa says the disturbance helped seal the end of the Central Avenue business corridor.
timeline.notes: City of Tampa Central Park CRA history: 'A racial disturbance in 1967 helped seal the demise of the Central Avenue business corridor.' Wikipedia 1967 Tampa riots: Martin Chambers, 19, shot by Patrolman James Calvert; 'The riots began on the night of June 11 and ended on June 15, in the neighborhood that was then known as Central Park'; Chambers 'was unarmed'. Coordinates: history-of-tampa point for the 1967 event.

timeline.title: Tampa International opens its landside-airside terminal
timeline.text: Tampa International Airport's new terminal opened to passengers on April 15, 1971, with a central landside building linked to four airside satellites, a landside-airside design described as the first of its type in the world.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'The terminal opened for passenger traffic on April 15, 1971 with four airside satellites (Airsides B, C, D, and E)'; 'Tampa International Airport's Landside/Airside terminal was the first of its type in the world.'

timeline.title: Franklin Street becomes a pedestrian mall
timeline.text: In 1973 Mayor Dick Greco led the groundbreaking for a pedestrian mall along five blocks of downtown Tampa's Franklin Street, as suburban malls drew shoppers away. Maas Brothers closed in 1991 and Woolworth in 1992, and in 2001 the re-elected Greco reopened the street to traffic.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27 (from history-of-tampa's franklin-mall and franklin-mall-reopened mapEvents; the cited Tampa Downtown Partnership report was re-opened). Report timeline: '1973 Mayor Dick Greco led the groundbreaking for a pedestrian mall along five blocks of Franklin Street'; '1991 Maas Brothers closes 1992 Woolworth closes 2001 Re-elected Mayor Greco reopened the pedestrian mall to vehicular traffic'; 'the competition created by suburban shopping centers and malls left Franklin Street underutilized'. Point is history-of-tampa's (on Franklin Street); tampa-theatre is the corridor landmark the report names.

timeline.title: St. Petersburg's inverted-pyramid Pier opens
timeline.text: The inverted-pyramid Pier replaced the Million Dollar Pier and opened in 1973; for four decades it was a symbol of St. Petersburg's waterfront.
timeline.notes: St. Pete Pier: 'It opened in 1973 and became a symbol of St. Petersburg's waterfront for four decades.' City: the 'Inverted Pyramid pier, a successor to the popular Million Dollar Pier'.

timeline.title: Ybor City's historic district is listed on the National Register
timeline.text: The Ybor City Historic District, mainly the 7th Avenue commercial corridor and its cigar factories, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974; a larger district was later designated a National Historic Landmark. The state bought the 1923 Ferlita Bakery in 1976 and opened it as the Ybor City State Museum in 1980.
timeline.notes: NHL nomination: 'National Register Historic District, listed in 1974, which includes mainly the 7th Avenue commercial corridor and adjoining cigar factories'; the NHL boundary adds residential areas. 'The State acquired the Ferlita Bakery in 1976, restored it, and opened it to the public as the Ybor City State Museum in 1980.' 'The bakery was built in 1923'. NPS place page: 'Designation: National Historic Landmark' (date not given).

timeline.title: The Rowdies win the Soccer Bowl in their first season
timeline.text: The Tampa Bay Rowdies, an expansion team in the North American Soccer League, won the league's Soccer Bowl in their 1975 inaugural season, beating the Portland Timbers 2-0 on Aug. 24; they played ten seasons at Tampa Stadium. That club folded in 1994; today's club of the same name plays at Al Lang Stadium in St. Petersburg.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. Wikipedia: 'The Rowdies played ten seasons at Tampa Stadium and won their only Soccer Bowl championship in their 1975 inaugural season, defeating the Portland Timbers 2-0 on August 24'; expansion franchise purchased June 19, 1974. The present club's Al Lang Stadium page: home since the 2011 season. No point: the final was played away from Tampa.

timeline.title: Pinellas County opens Heritage Village
timeline.text: Pinellas County's history museum, Heritage Village in Largo, has served visitors since 1976; its historic buildings, gathered from around the county, include the 1924 Gandy Tower that marked the entrance to the Gandy Bridge, an 1850s log cabin from Clearwater's founding families and a 1930s Tarpon Springs sponge warehouse.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. Point from the see-pinellas place record.

timeline.title: The Buccaneers play their first NFL season
timeline.text: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers played their first NFL season in 1976 at Tampa Stadium under coach John McKay and did not win a game (0-14). Tampa Stadium, opened in 1967, was their home until Raymond James Stadium was built next to it in 1998; the old stadium was demolished in 1999.

Raymond James: 'built at public expense as a replacement for Tampa Stadium', opened 1998. timeline.title: A freighter brings down the Sunshine Skyway
timeline.text: On the morning of May 9, 1980, during a sudden squall, the freighter Summit Venture struck a support pier of the Sunshine Skyway's southbound span. More than 1,200 feet of the span fell, and 35 people died when vehicles, including a Greyhound bus, plunged into Tampa Bay; one driver survived the fall.

timeline.title: The Dalí Museum opens in St. Petersburg
timeline.text: A. Reynolds and Eleanor Morse collected Salvador Dalí's work from 1943, and when they decided in the mid-1970s to give their collection away, St. Petersburg rallied to bring it to the city. The Dalí Museum opened in St. Petersburg in 1982.
timeline.notes: The Dalí: 'On March 21, 1943, the Morses bought their first Dalí painting'; 'by the mid-1970s decided to donate their entire collection. A Wall Street Journal article... caught the attention of the St. Petersburg, FL community, who rallied to bring the collection to the area. The Dalí Museum, St. Petersburg, FL opened in 1982.'  No coordinates: the 1982 building is not the current one and its site is not given.

timeline.title: The new Sunshine Skyway opens
timeline.text: A new Sunshine Skyway, with a tall cable-stayed center span and safety features added because of the 1980 disaster to protect it from ship collisions, opened in 1987. The old bridge was partly demolished and converted into two long fishing piers, now Skyway Fishing Pier State Park.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'The current Sunshine Skyway opened in 1987 and is the second bridge of that name on the site'; 'Owing to the 1980 disaster, the current bridge incorporates numerous safety features to protect the structure from ship collisions'; the text gives both January 11, 1987 (opened to runners) and an April 30, 1987 opening ceremony, so only the year is used. Same article: 'a pair of long beam bridges with a central tall cable-stayed bridge'; 'the old bridge was partially demolished and converted into two long fishing piers'; 'converted into a long pier for newly created Skyway Fishing Pier State Park'. | Verifier 2026-09-27: linked the see-pinellas sunshine-skyway-bridge place and used its point and area (south-stpete) so the bridge and its history sit on the same sheet; the old bridge's remains are Skyway Fishing Pier State Park.

timeline.title: Tampa's performing arts center opens
timeline.text: The Tampa Bay Performing Arts Center opened in July 1987 at a cost of $57 million. Renamed the Straz Center in 2009, it is owned by the City of Tampa.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'It opened in July 1987 at a cost of $57 million as the Tampa Bay Performing Arts Center. It was renamed in 2009. The Straz Center is owned by the City of Tampa and operated by the David A. [Straz Jr. Center...]'. strazcenter.org is behind a bot wall.

timeline.title: The Tampa Convention Center opens on the Fort Brooke site
timeline.text: The Tampa Convention Center opened in October 1990 on the waterfront land where Fort Brooke had stood, replacing the aging Curtis Hixon Hall; the city paid the $140 million cost with municipal bonds.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27 (history-of-tampa's convention-center mapEvent; its Tampa Bay Times archive citation is paywalled). Wikipedia: 'The former location of the fort was used for various industrial and commercial purposes until the late 1980s, when it was cleared to make way for a new convention center to replace Tampa's aging Curtis Hixon Hall'; 'the city of Tampa paying the $140 million cost by issuing municipal bonds'; 'It opened in October 1990.' Point from the venues-bay place record.

timeline.title: St. Petersburg's dome is finished as the city courts big-league baseball
timeline.text: The Florida Suncoast Dome in St. Petersburg, part of the city's effort to attract Major League Baseball, was finished in 1990, before it had a tenant. The Lightning played there as the ThunderDome from 1993 to 1996, and after Major League Baseball awarded the area a franchise in 1995 the building became Tropicana Field, home of the Rays.
timeline.notes: Tropicana Field (Wikipedia): 'Tropicana Field opened in 1990 and was originally known as the Florida Suncoast Dome'; 'still had no tenants'; 'In 1993, the Tampa Bay Lightning moved to the facility and its name was changed to the ThunderDome until the team moved to its new home in downtown Tampa in 1996.' Rays: franchise approved March 9, 1995. Tropicana Field (Wikipedia): 'City officials decided early on that the city would attempt to attract Major League Baseball.'

timeline.title: The Pinellas Trail opens on an old rail line
timeline.text: After CSX abandoned 34 miles of track in Pinellas County in the 1980s, the state bought the corridor, and the first 5 miles of the Pinellas Trail opened in December 1990. Much of the trail follows the roadbed of the Orange Belt Railway, the county's first railroad.
timeline.notes: Pinellas Trail (Wikipedia): 'After the SCL joined CSX Transportation in the 1980s, 34 mi of trackage in Pinellas County was abandoned, and purchased by the Florida Department of Transportation'; 'The first 5 mi opened in December 1990'. Dunedin (Wikipedia): 'A large portion of the trail lies on the former roadbed of the Orange Belt Railway, the first railroad in Pinellas County, which arrived in 1888.'

timeline.title: The Lightning play their first NHL game
timeline.text: The Tampa Bay Lightning, founded as an NHL expansion team in 1990, played their first regular-season game on Oct. 7, 1992, in Expo Hall at the Florida State Fairgrounds, before moving to the ThunderDome in St. Petersburg in 1993 and to their downtown Tampa arena in 1996.
timeline.notes: Lightning (Wikipedia): 'founded as an expansion team on December 6, 1990, and began play in the 1992–93 NHL season'; 'The Lightning played their first regular season game on October 7, 1992, in Tampa's Expo Hall at the Florida State Fairgrounds.' Tropicana Field: ThunderDome 1993-1996.

timeline.title: The Florida Aquarium opens in the Channel District
timeline.text: The Florida Aquarium opened in Tampa on March 31, 1995, and says it served one million residents and visitors in its first year of operation.
timeline.notes: Florida Aquarium About Us (WebFetch): 'The Florida Aquarium opened in Tampa on March 31, 1995'; first-year impact 'serving over one million residents and visitors'. | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'more than a million' -> 'one million' (the aquarium's words).

timeline.title: The Ice Palace arena opens downtown
timeline.text: The county-owned arena in downtown Tampa opened in 1996 as the Ice Palace, home of the Lightning. Later called the St. Pete Times Forum, Tampa Bay Times Forum and Amalie Arena, it took the name Benchmark International Arena in 2025.
timeline.notes: City of Tampa proclamation (Aug 13, 2025): 'formally known first as the Ice Palace, then the St. Pete Times Forum, Tampa Bay Times Forum and Amalie Arena, has served as the heart of Tampa's vibrant downtown since its opening in 1996'; 'a county-owned facility'; home of the Lightning's regular-season games. Renaming year 2025 from the proclamation's date and subject.

timeline.title: The Yankees open their Tampa spring ballpark
timeline.text: The New York Yankees' spring training park in Tampa opened on March 1, 1996, as Legends Field; renamed George M. Steinbrenner Field in 2008, it is also home to the Yankees' Florida State League affiliate, the Tampa Tarpons, and was the Tampa Bay Rays' home for the 2025 season.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27. Wikipedia infobox: opened March 1, 1996; former names Legends Field (1996-2008); home of the Tampa Tarpons; temporary home of the Rays in 2025. Yankees page: 'Built in 1996', spring home of the Yankees and summer home of the Tampa Tarpons. Point from the venues-bay place record.

timeline.title: Big-league baseball arrives and the Bucs get a new stadium
timeline.text: The Tampa Bay Devil Rays, awarded to the area in 1995 after nearly three decades of trying, played the first regular-season game at Tropicana Field on March 31, 1998, losing 11-6 to the Detroit Tigers; the team became simply the Rays after the 2007 season. Raymond James Stadium, with its pirate ship in the north end zone, also opened in 1998 in Tampa as the Buccaneers' new home.
timeline.notes: Rays (Wikipedia): 'Following nearly three decades of unsuccessfully trying... an ownership group led by Vince Naimoli was approved on March 9, 1995'; 'The Devil Rays played their first game on March 31, 1998, against the Detroit Tigers at Tropicana Field, before an opening day crowd of 45,369'; name changed to Rays after the 2007 season. Raymond James (Wikipedia): opened 1998, 'known for the replica pirate ship located behind the seating area in the north end zone'. | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'before 45,369 fans' was the 1998 capacity, not a stated attendance; replaced by the result from the Tropicana Field article.

timeline.title: Streetcars return between downtown and Ybor City
timeline.text: The TECO Line Streetcar opened on Oct. 19, 2002, with replica Birney cars running between downtown Tampa, the Channel District and Ybor City. A 0.3-mile extension in December 2010 brought the line to 2.7 miles.
timeline.notes: City of Tampa: 'The TECO Line Streetcar is a 2.7 mile long fixed guideway transit system... connects downtown Tampa, with the Channelside District and Ybor City Historic District. The first 2.4-mile-long segment opened for service in 2002 while a 0.3-mile-long extension opened for service in December 2010.' TBHC: 'became operational on Oct. 19, 2002'; replica Birney cars.

timeline.title: The Buccaneers win Super Bowl XXXVII
timeline.text: On Jan. 26, 2003, in San Diego, the Buccaneers beat the Oakland Raiders 48-21 in Super Bowl XXXVII, the franchise's first Super Bowl title.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'played on January 26, 2003, at Qualcomm Stadium in San Diego'; 'The Buccaneers defeated the Raiders by the score of 48–21... winning their first-ever Super Bowl'; 'This was the first professional sports championship ever won by a Tampa-based team.' No coordinates: the game was in San Diego. | Verifier 2026-09-27: dropped 'the first professional sports championship won by a Tampa-based team' (Wikipedia's claim conflicts with the Tampa Bay Rowdies' 1975 Soccer Bowl title, now its own record).

timeline.title: The Lightning win their first Stanley Cup
timeline.text: The Lightning beat the Calgary Flames in seven games to win their first Stanley Cup on June 7, 2004, clinching Game 7 at home, 2-1; they were then the southernmost team ever to win it.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: dates May 25 - June 7, 2004; 'defeated the Western Conference champion Calgary Flames in seven games for their first Stanley Cup in franchise history, becoming the southernmost team to win the Stanley Cup until... Florida Panthers won the Cup in 2024.' Game 7 was played at the St. Pete Times Forum in Tampa (game box stadium1), where the Cup was presented after the Lightning's 2-1 win.

timeline.title: The Rays win their first pennant
timeline.text: In 2008 the Rays had their first winning season, won the American League East and their first American League pennant, beating the Boston Red Sox, before losing the World Series to the Philadelphia Phillies. They won another pennant in 2020.
timeline.notes: Rays (Wikipedia): 'The 2008 season saw the Rays post their first winning season, their first AL East championship, and their first American League pennant (defeating the rival Boston Red Sox in the ALCS), though they lost to the Philadelphia Phillies in that year's World Series'; 'another American League pennant again in 2020'.

timeline.title: The Tampa Bay History Center opens on the waterfront
timeline.text: The Tampa Bay History Center opened its museum at 801 Water Street in the Channel District on Jan. 17, 2009.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'The museum is on the waterfront at 801 Water Street in Tampa's Channelside District. It opened on January 17, 2009.'

timeline.title: A new art museum and park open on the Riverwalk
timeline.text: In 2010 Curtis Hixon Waterfront Park, a new Tampa Museum of Art building and the Glazer Children's Museum opened together on the downtown riverfront, a milestone for the Riverwalk. The art museum, which opened its first exhibit in 1920, held its grand opening on Feb. 6, 2010.
timeline.notes: Tampa Museum of Art (Wikipedia): 'The museum opened its first exhibit on November 22, 1920 when the institution was called the Tampa Museum of Fine Arts'; 'the grand opening of the new Tampa Museum of Art took place on February 6, 2010'. Tampa Riverwalk (Wikipedia): 'The project reached a significant milestone in 2010 when Curtis Hixon Waterfront Park, a new Tampa Museum of Art, and the Glazer Children's Museum all opened'.

timeline.title: The Dalí Museum opens its new building
timeline.text: The Dalí Museum opened its new building at One Dali Boulevard in St. Petersburg on Jan. 11, 2011, built to better protect and display a collection that now numbers more than 2,400 works.
timeline.notes: The Dalí: 'The distinguished new building, which opened on January 11, 2011, enables the Museum to better protect and display the collection'; 'The collection includes over 2,400 works'. Address One Dali Blvd from the see-pinellas record (dali-museum).

timeline.title: Tampa hosts the Republican National Convention
timeline.text: The 2012 Republican National Convention met at the downtown arena, then the Tampa Bay Times Forum, in the week of Aug. 27, 2012, and nominated Mitt Romney and Paul Ryan. Hurricane Isaac's approach forced organizers to recess the first day.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'The convention was held during the week of August 27, 2012, in Tampa, Florida at the Tampa Bay Times Forum (now Benchmark International Arena)'; nominated Romney and Ryan; 'the convention came to order on August 27, 2012, and then immediately recessed until the following afternoon because of the risk of Isaac hitting Tampa.'

timeline.title: Encore rises on the site of the Scrub
timeline.text: The Ella, the first building of the Encore development, opened in December 2012 on land that had been the Scrub and then the Central Park Village housing project. The City's Soulwalk markers now tell the neighborhood's history.
timeline.notes: Soulwalk marker: Central Park Village replaced by Encore; 'The Ella, opened in December 2012'. Raw marker text: 'Central Park Village was itself replaced by Encore!, The first building of the new development, The Ella, opened in December 2012.' Coordinates: history-of-tampa's point for The Ella.

timeline.title: The Tampa Riverwalk is completed to Water Works Park
timeline.text: The Riverwalk grew from a 1970s boardwalk; a boardwalk under the Kennedy Boulevard bridge joined its segments into one continuous path, and a 2016 extension past the Straz Center and under I-275 to Water Works Park brought it to its present 2.6 miles, from the Channel District to Armature Works.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'Tampa's Riverwalk has its origins in the 1970s'; 'In 2014, a federal transportation grant was used to complete a $9.2 million boardwalk under the Kennedy Boulevard bridge, connecting all existing segments into one continuous path' (history-of-tampa dates the connection to March 27, 2015 from a Tampa Bay Times article that could not be read; the year is left out); 'A further northward extension completed in 2016 stretched the path past the Straz Center... and under Interstate 275 to newly opened Waterworks Park... bringing the total length of the Riverwalk to 2.6 mile.' Riverwalk FAQ: 'extends 2.6 miles from Armature Works to Sparkman Wharf'.

timeline.title: Sparkman Wharf opens in the old Channelside Bay Plaza
timeline.text: Sparkman Wharf, an outdoor dining and entertainment spot on the water built in the former Channelside Bay Plaza, opened on Nov. 30, 2018. The wharf is named for Stephen M. Sparkman, the congressman who brought federal money in 1905 to dredge deep-water channels to the Channelside area.
timeline.notes: Tampa Bay Times photo caption (the article body is paywalled; only the headline and caption were readable): 'the new Sparkman Wharf, formerly Channelside Bay Plaza... Strategic Property Planners, LLC, a Tampa-based real estate development company, prepare to open Tampa's newest mixed-use waterfront destination for outdoor dining and entertainment on Friday, November 30, 2018.' The see-tampa slice places Sparkman Wharf 'at Water Street Tampa' (source sparkmanwharf.com); the developer's name is left out because the caption's 'Strategic Property Planners' differs from history-of-tampa's 'Strategic Property Partners'. History of Tampa (Wikipedia): 'In 1905, Stephen M. Sparkman... brought in federal money to dig deep-water channels from Port Tampa to Channelside... In 2018, Sparkman Wharf was named for him.'

timeline.title: Water Street Tampa's first towers open
timeline.text: Water Street Tampa, a mixed-use district whose first phase began in 2017, opened the JW Marriott Tampa Water Street in 2020, the 100th JW Marriott hotel, and its first residential tower, Heron, in April 2021; a second phase is expected by 2027.
timeline.notes: Verifier addition 2026-09-27 (scope item 'Water Street'). Wikipedia: 'Phase one of the development of Water Street began in 2017 and phase two is expected to be completed in 2027'; 'Water Street opened its first mixed-use residential building, Heron Residences, in April 2021'; 'The JW Marriott opened in the Water Street neighborhood in 2020, making it the 100th hotel built by JW Marriott.' Point from the see-tampa place record.

timeline.title: The new St. Pete Pier opens
timeline.text: The inverted-pyramid Pier closed in 2013, and the new 26-acre St. Pete Pier district opened on July 6, 2020, with restaurants, public art, green space and a 1,380-foot pier.
timeline.notes: St. Pete Pier (raw page): 'The structure closed in 2013 to make way for a new St. Petersburg Pier'; 'The new 26-acre Pier District opened on July 6, 2020. Today, it is home to seven restaurants, public art installations... that stretch across the 1,380-foot pier.'

timeline.title: The Lightning win the Stanley Cup in the Edmonton bubble
timeline.text: Playing the entire Final without fans in Edmonton because of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Lightning beat the Dallas Stars and won their second Stanley Cup on Sept. 28, 2020.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the entire series was played behind closed doors at Rogers Place in Edmonton'; dates September 19-28, 2020; Vasilevskiy shutout clinched in Game 6. No coordinates (played in Edmonton).

timeline.title: The Buccaneers win Super Bowl LV at home
timeline.text: On Feb. 7, 2021, the Buccaneers, led by quarterback Tom Brady in his first season with the team, beat the Kansas City Chiefs 31-9 in Super Bowl LV at Raymond James Stadium, the first time a team played a Super Bowl in its home stadium.
timeline.notes: Wikipedia: 'defeated the defending Super Bowl and AFC champions Kansas City Chiefs, 31–9'; 'played on February 7, 2021, at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, the home stadium of the Buccaneers, marking the first time a team played a Super Bowl in its home stadium'; Brady 'in his first season away from the New England Patriots'.

timeline.title: The Lightning repeat as champions at home
timeline.text: On July 7, 2021, the Lightning beat the Montreal Canadiens 1-0 in Game 5 at their home arena in Tampa to win their second straight Stanley Cup and third overall.
timeline.notes: 2021 Final (Wikipedia): Game 5 July 7 at Amalie Arena (the game box lists stadium1=Amalie Arena, Tampa Bay home); 'The Stanley Cup was presented to Lightning captain Steven Stamkos... following the Lightning's 1–0 win in Game 5.' Lightning: Cups in 2004, 2020 and 2021.

timeline.title: Hurricane Helene's surge floods the Pinellas beaches
timeline.text: Hurricane Helene made landfall far to the north in Florida's Big Bend on the night of Sept. 26, 2024, but its storm surge flooded the Tampa Bay coast with 5 to 7 feet of water above ground, setting a record at St. Petersburg's tide gauge. Twelve people drowned in Pinellas County, most on the barrier islands from St. Pete Beach to Indian Rocks Beach, and at least 419 homes were destroyed in Pinellas and Hillsborough counties.
timeline.notes: NHC Tropical Cyclone Report (Helene): landfall 'about 10 n mi southwest of Perry, Florida, around 0310 UTC 27 September' (the night of Sept. 26 local time); 'Maximum storm surge inundation of 5 to 7 ft AGL occurred from the Anclote River southward to Longboat Key'; 'Within Tampa Bay, maximum storm surge inundation of 5 to 7 ft AGL occurred'; the St. Petersburg tide station's 6.31 ft above MHHW 'surpassed the previous record of 3.97 ft during Hurricane Elena (1985)'; 'In Pinellas County, 12 people drowned in the surge. Media reports indicate that 9 of these 12 victims were located on the barrier islands on Pinellas County's west coast from St. Pete Beach to Indian Rocks Beach'; 'Helene destroyed at least 419 homes in Pinellas and Hillsborough Counties combined'. The report gives Madeira Beach 7.26 ft above MHHW. Coordinates: Madeira Beach (Photon).

timeline.title: Hurricane Milton strikes Siesta Key and tears the roof off the Trop
timeline.text: Two weeks after Helene, Hurricane Milton made landfall on Siesta Key near Sarasota on the night of Oct. 9, 2024, as a Category 3 storm, causing major damage in the Sarasota and Tampa Bay areas. Its winds ripped off most of Tropicana Field's fabric roof, and more than 20 inches of rain fell near St. Petersburg, bringing record crests on the Hillsborough River.
timeline.notes: NHC TCR (Milton): 'made landfall on the west coast of the Florida peninsula as a category 3 hurricane, causing major damage in the Sarasota and Tampa Bay areas'; 'landfall on Siesta Key, Florida, at 0030 UTC 10 October' (8:30 p.m. Oct. 9 EDT); 'the Tropicana Field stadium in St. Petersburg, where the fabric roof was ripped off by high winds'; 'the area of the Florida west coast most affected by Milton had also been affected by Hurricane Helene two weeks before'; 'rainfall was 20.40 inches at a CoCoRaHS site near St. Petersburg'; 'widespread river and urban flooding, particularly in the St. Petersburg-Tampa area where record-high crests were recorded on the Hillsborough River'. WUSF: 'The winds ripped off most of the roof'.

timeline.title: The Rays play a season in Tampa at Steinbrenner Field
timeline.text: With Tropicana Field under repair, the Rays played their 2025 home games at George M. Steinbrenner Field in Tampa, the Yankees' spring training park, outdoors in the summer weather.
timeline.notes: WUSF: 'after a season in the summer elements at their temporary digs of Steinbrenner Field in Tampa'. MLB Yankees page (opened): 'Built in 1996, George M. Steinbrenner Field is a 31-acre complex... spring home to the New York Yankees'.

timeline.title: The Rays come home to a repaired Tropicana Field
timeline.text: After more than 18 months of repairs costing the City of St. Petersburg nearly $60 million, Tropicana Field reopened on April 6, 2026, when the Rays beat the Chicago Cubs 6-4 in their home opener. The team's new owners plan a ballpark next to Steinbrenner Field on Hillsborough College's Dale Mabry campus in Tampa.
timeline.notes: WUSF (published April 5, 2026, a Sunday): 'Tampa Bay hosts the Chicago Cubs on Monday in the Rays' 2026 home opener' → date 2026-04-06 derived from the publication date; 'more than 18 months of repairs'; 'nearly $60 million was spent by the city to make it baseball-ready'; 'the lease running out in 2028'; 'on the clock to build a new ballpark next to Steinbrenner Field on Hillsborough College's Dale Mabry campus'. | Verifier 2026-09-27: 'the team's lease runs through 2028' is not in the WUSF article, removed; the April 6 date and 6-4 result are in Wikipedia's Tropicana Field article (also confirms the Monday opener).

timeline.title: Tampa Theatre turns 100
timeline.text: Tampa Theatre, which opened on Oct. 15, 1926, marks 100 years to the day on Oct. 15, 2026, with a Centennial Celebration at the theatre (listed as sold out), capping an anniversary week that includes a public open house on Oct. 11 and classic film screenings Oct. 12-14.
timeline.notes: The anniversary date is arithmetic from the opening date (Oct 15, 1926, Wikipedia). No centennial program was confirmed: tampatheatre.org serves a bot challenge and returned an empty page to WebFetch, and web search was unavailable in this session. 'shows films and hosts concerts and tours': venues-bay record (the theatre's own Visit Tampa Bay listing text). Events slices should add dated centennial events if the theatre announces them. | Verifier 2026-09-27: tampatheatre.org is readable through WebFetch. The Centennial Celebration page: 'On October 15, 1926, Tampa Theatre opened its doors...', Thursday, October 15, doors 6:00pm, $26 + taxes and fees, 'THIS EVENT IS SOLD OUT'; the home page lists the Oct. 11 open house and the Oct. 12-14 screenings (Casablanca, The Wizard of Oz, A Night at the Opera).

report:
# Timeline slice: report (checked 2026-09-27)

## What this slice holds

- **115 timeline milestones** across the seven eras: indigenous 4, spanish 5, frontier 16, boomtown 24, land-boom 18, postwar 18, modern 30.
- By region (derived from `area`): Tampa 61, St. Petersburg 23, Clearwater & North Pinellas 12, Day Trips 10, Gulf Beaches 5, Around the Bay 4.
- 92 records carry coordinates, 92 link to at least one place id, 65 carry at least one image.
- **74 media records** (all `subject_kind: "timeline"`): public domain 44, CC BY-SA 21, CC BY 8, US government 1. No GFDL, FAL, fair-use or non-commercial files.
- **8 facts**: Census Bureau Vintage 2025 population estimates (Tampa 413,554; St. Petersburg 264,033; Clearwater 114,364; Tampa-St. Petersburg-Clearwater metro 3,418,895; Hillsborough 1,574,115; Pinellas 948,563, all July 1, 2025), Pinellas County's 2020 Census count (959,107, quoted from the county), and Tampa's 1880 and 1900 census counts (720 and 15,839).

## How the candidates were found

WebSearch was unavailable for the whole session (the shared session had used its 200-search budget before this slice started), so discovery used other routes:

1. **history-of-tampa** (`js/data.js` mapEvents, events, scrollSteps, eraMilestones, mediaAssets, historicStreetcar; `js/ybor-data.js` mapEvents and mediaAssets). Every cited original was re-opened: the City Clerk's incorporation history, the Henry B. Plant Museum chronology, the NPS Ybor City NHL nomination (PDF, text extracted), the NPS Teaching with Historic Places lesson 51 (PDF), the LoC Ybor City guide, NPS Tampa Bay Hotel, the Soulwalk markers (Woolworth, Scrub), the Central Park CRA history, the North Franklin Street NRHP form (PDF), the Museum of Florida History shipbuilding page, the TBHC streetcar blog, the City's streetcar page, and the 2025 arena proclamation. Items whose cited page could not be read (Tampa Bay Times archive articles are paywalled; the Florida Aquarium proclamation URL now returns HTML; the 1990 Convention Center opening) were re-sourced or left out.
2. **Official history pages found by browsing site navigation**: stpete.org/visitors/history.php (a rich city history, including Black history), stpetepier.org/history, thevinoy.com/history, doncesar.com/history, ymkg.com (Gasparilla), flstrawberryfestival.com, plantcitygov.com, spongedocks.net (Tarpon Springs), hcfl.gov county history, pinellas.gov facts and park pages, usf.edu history, thedali.org, ringling.org, flsouthern.edu, flaquarium.org, opalcollection.com (Belleview Inn), historyandnature.org (Fort Foster), weedonislandpreserve.org, the MLB Phillies and Yankees ballpark pages, NPS De Soto National Memorial.
3. **Primary government data**: NHC Tropical Cyclone Reports for Helene (AL092024) and Milton (AL142024); Census Bureau Vintage 2025 CSVs (sub-est2025.csv, cbsa-est2025-alldata.csv) from www2.census.gov; the 1960 Census of Population, Florida volume (Table 5).
4. **Wikipedia as discovery and, where no official page could be read, as the source**: History of Tampa (for leads), then the specific articles. 54 of 115 records use a Wikipedia article as `source_url`; most of these are Civil War actions, Seminole Wars, bridges, sports championships and events whose official pages block automated readers (floridastateparks.org, tampaairport.com, macdill.af.mil, census.gov QuickFacts, strazcenter.org, tampatheatre.org, myclearwater.com and dunedingov.com all returned 403 or a bot challenge).
5. **Other slices' records** (history-tampa, history-region, see-*, venues-bay, outdoors, stays-*) for shared place ids and coordinates, and to link milestones to places (for example Cotanchobee Fort Brooke Park, Oaklawn Cemetery, the Ybor Factory Building, Parque Amigos de José Martí, the Detroit Hotel site, the World's First Airline monument, the Manhattan Casino).
6. **Media**: history-of-tampa's mediaAssets (licenses re-read from the Commons API), plus files named in the Wikipedia articles above, all license-checked in batches through the Commons imageinfo API (LicenseShortName, Artist, date, size). Two files needed the Commons file page itself (Belleview postcard: Florida Memory, public domain under Florida Statutes 257.35(6); sponge harvest: location confirmed as Tarpon Springs).

Every record's facts were checked against the raw page text (curl or extracted PDF text) wherever WebFetch's summary was used, after a WebFetch summary misreported the Ringling Museum's dates. Notes on each record quote the sentences the text rests on.

## Coordinates

Census geocoder address matches or Photon name matches from `research/tools/geocode.mjs` (checked against the matched text), or the coordinates already in other slices for the same place id. Several Tampa points reuse history-of-tampa's positions (the Scrub, the 1967 disturbance, The Ella, the village of Tampa). Records about wide areas, towns or events away from a fixed site (county formation, incorporations, Gasparilla, championships played elsewhere) have no coordinates.

## Left out, and why

- Luis de Cáncer (1549) and the Cuban fishing ranchos as separate milestones: no readable source found (the Cáncer articles 404ed; the ranchos appear only as one sentence in the History of Tampa article, used inside the 1763 record).
- Crystal River's mound complex (occupied from about the 2nd century AD): the only readable source gives no clean year; Florida State Parks pages are blocked.
- Paleo-Indian settlement and the formation of Tampa Bay about 6,000 years ago: Wikipedia's figures conflict with its Manasota article; left out rather than guess a year.
- The 1968 St. Petersburg sanitation strike, Clearwater's Fort Harrison (dates conflict: 1835 vs 1841), Gamble Plantation and Judah Benjamin (1865), the Anclote Key lighthouse (1887), the Tampa Convention Center (1990), Armature Works' 2018 opening, Water Street Tampa's groundbreaking, and Winter the dolphin: no readable page, conflicting dates, or not re-sourced in time.
- The Tampa Theatre centennial program: tampatheatre.org serves a bot challenge; the 2026 record states only that Oct. 15, 2026 is the 100th anniversary of the opening date.
- History-of-tampa's DERIVED items (the 1915 phosphate peak, the 1955 Central Avenue apex) were not reused.

## Open questions for the verifier

1. **Conflicting dates kept as year only**: the Davis Causeway (Jan. 28 vs June 28, 1934), the new Sunshine Skyway (Jan. 11 vs April 30, 1987), Busch Gardens (March 31 vs June 1, 1959), the Riverwalk's continuous link (2014 in Wikipedia, March 27, 2015 in history-of-tampa's unreadable Tampa Bay Times source).
2. **Owner's date vs other sources**: the Belleview (1896 per the Opal Collection, 1897 per Wikipedia); the Sponge Exchange (1907 per spongedocks.net, often given as 1908); Centro Asturiano (1902 NHL table vs 1904 NPS lesson).
3. **Rays 2026 home opener date** (2026-04-06) is derived from WUSF's April 5 article saying the opener is "on Monday".
4. **Deuces record** uses year 1960 to stand for "the 1960s" (no single event), with `date` left empty.
